subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
That this House condemn the government for its signing of a trade
agreement with the United States that, amongst other things:
(a)	fails to consider the disproportionate effect on women, and especially the loss of jobs in the service sector where women are concentrated;
(b)	will give up provincial control over energy resources in a continental energy market; and
(c)	fails to allow for adequate consultation with Canadians in all provinces and territories before committing us to profound changes not only in our economy, but our political sovereignty, cultural distinctiveness and generally, our ability to run our own affairs.
She said: Mr. Speaker, it is not with very much pleasure that I rise to speak to this motion this morning. As a matter of fact, it is with lament and concern about what is the future of my country.
When we talk about any type of economic strategy for Canada, we must talk about an economic strategy for women. Sixty per cent of the jobs in textiles, shoes, and leather are held by women. We recognize that this will take massive readjustment.
The whole debate that has taken place on the accord is something that is of great concern because of the direction that it has taken. Often we say that this is a great new way for Canada to open up its doors, but what we are really looking at is a massive change in direction socially, economically, and politically in our country. I do not think that this Government has the mandate to do that without any discussion with the Canadian people.
The whole episode of the hearings yesterday in Vancouver demonstrated that a province as large as British Columbia, with as many resources as Vancouver, was treated as if it did not count. It was calculated that one group received 10 seconds to be heard. That is not the way that we have conducted business in this country. It is not the way that Canadians wish to be heard. We do not like our participation being treated as an insult to our intelligence, that we cannot understand it and are not capable of participating for more than 10 seconds.

November 24, 1987
Supply
One thing at which we must look very seriously is that we have always displayed a great deal of participation when it comes to some kind of new direction. When we talk about participation-and we do not even have the final text in front of us-we know that hundreds of thousands of women's jobs are threatened. At the same time we do not even have time to critique it in detail, because the Government refuses to give us that detail.
It is very interesting that the Macdonald Commission travelled across the country and spent many years and hundreds of thousands of dollars looking in depth at what would be the future economy of the country. It heard repeatedly that the main issue in Canada was employment. It wanted to know that jobs were possible, that employment was possible. The Government chose to ignore it, and the Macdonald Commission came out with a recommendation to go for some kind of an agreement with the United States which would tie us more heavily to the direction the United States was taking. This morning I would like to look particularly this morning at what are the implications of the studies which have been done and, more importantly, the studies which have not been done, on the effects of the whole agreement. We feel very strongly about an agreement in the service sector. I think it is important to recognize that there has never been any kind of free trade agreement in the service sector with any other country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: You are absolutely right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Of course I am right. When the Economic Council of Canada did its study, it did not take the service sector into account, because it said that there was no way that that would be a component of it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: It has it on its agenda.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Yes, it has it on its agenda because the Government put it on the agenda. We know what are the implications of that.
I am always very interested to hear members of the Government talking about the service sector. They say that hairdressers or schoolteachers are not going to move from one country to another.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Who said that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I have heard many members of the Conservative Party say that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Name one.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, the very same thing was said at the committee last week. Perhaps members of the Government do not understand what is the service sector. It includes data processing, data collection, and banking. Some of the things at which we look in the service sector not only implicate a lot of jobs for women, but they also implicate a lot of jobs and flow of information in Canadian security.
We must recognize that as early as 1976 the Canadian Government was beginning to sense that the free flow of information across borders could be a threat to our sovereignty. We also know that under the Bank Act we have insisted that that information be collected on Canadian grounds. It is very important from a privacy of information point of view, as well as the need of our own economy, to have some kind of dependence. It has been well established that free flow of information increases dependence on another country instead of increasing our interdependence, and there is a big difference in those two approaches.
[ Translation]
It is very important, when considering the outcome of free trade, that we should review the impact free trade will have on women. We already know that the industries where jobs are most threatened are those which employ mostly women. In such industries as textile, clothing, leathergoods and footwear, where jobs are held mostly by women a massive job loss is to be expected.
According to a study carried out in Ontario, this province alone will lose over 100,000 jobs now held by women. But it is quite clear that this phenomenon will not be limited to Ontario. In the province of Quebec, the textile industry is a major employer of women. By signing the free trade agreement now before the House, the Conservative Government is depriving these women of their means of existence and permanently reducing their standard of living.
These women will not be easily retrained and returned to the labour market. Most of the women working in manufacturing industries are older women. What will the Conservative Government say to these Canadian women who, unfortunately, do not have the flexibility expected of them? Does the Government seriously think that these women, having worked for many years in a plant and acquired only the skills connected with their jobs, will gladly accept to lose their jobs as a show of support for this free trade deal!
What will the Government say to all the immigrant women working in industries which are being threatened by the Reagan-Mulroney Agreement? These women are often at a disavantage because of linguistic problems which will have a negative effect on their retraining. Because of their generally lower level of education they will not have access to many fields of activity in the labour market. These women have families to support; they cannot afford to remain unemployed for very long. Up against such insurmontable odds how will they be able to get into a retraining program?
This Government must consider the retraining issue as irrelevant, because it has failed to include in the agreement any guarantees for women who are likely to lose their jobs. We are still waiting for retraining programs which are supposed to help the Canadian men and women who will be the losers as a result of the Reagan-Mulroney Agreement. How long will these women have to wait before they can again support their families?
November 24, 1987



It really is quite a shock when they talk about readjustment programs and when I have heard Mr. Lipsey say that of course there will be higher paid jobs and ask why women are worried about lower paid ones.
Single parents are looking at the future implications on their families. Some are using all their energies today to survive. They recognize that with just some signatures and a lot of fanfare suddenly their ability to earn a living, to feed their children, and to live in their communities with some dignity, is gone. That is the kind of thing the Government is doing to the people of Canada.
More than that, we are talking about something which is very ethical-the ethics of participation in terms of allowing the people of Canada to know what is their future. It is all very well for members of the Government to say that there has never been a free trade agreement in the service industry. However, they have not bothered to study it. Nor have they bothered to say what are the implications for the people in that industry.
The flow of information going from Canada to the United States is higher than that flowing from the United States into Canada. We also know that American corporations made a decision last year to do all their production scheduling and evaluations out of their American headquarters. We also know that in one little office in Brantford the jobs were reduced from 23 to 5. That is the implication for company after company. Those are the kinds of things which need to be looked at, but government Members do not talk about them.
I am a little tired of hearing about the effects of the free trade agreement on Ontario. I cannot believe that government Members really do not understand what is the Auto Pact. The Auto Pact involves protection for equal partners in an agreement. There is no suggestion that that kind of fairness will take place in the service industry. There is no suggestion that the jobs and lives of women implicated in this regard will have any kind of protection; nor have they bothered to study it. That in itself is unethical and wrong. It really says that they do not count.
If we listen closely to the debate, we hear them saying that the market forces will be the ones to direct it. We all know what the market forces can do and how vulnerable people become in that regard. However, what worries me more than that is that when we talk about market forces and supply and demand, we are really talking about people's lives and their futures as commodities, and that if they do not fit into it we will just dispense with them.
What do we come to, Madam Speaker? We come to the survival of the fittest. It means that competitiveness is the first priority. Then you dispose of any human being who does not fit into that category. It means profit only for multinationals.
Supply
That is basically what we are talking about, but that is not the character or the direction of the country.
In the 120 years of our history we have said very clearly that there is a potential for us to do something different. We are smaller than our neighbours south of the border. We want to be good friends with them but we want to do things our way with our ethic and value system. Because we want to do it our way with our own ethic and value system, it helps the Americans to be different from us and it helps us to be different from them. With that we are both strengthened.
This new foolish, foolish agreement before us-at least what we have of it because all we have is a "no-review", and we have no detail-is saying that the only way Canadians will survive economically is to tie ourselves firmly and strongly in one direction and that is south of the border.
Just think for a minute or two about data flow, information flow. If that starts to flow back and forth north and south with no regulation, and that seems to be the implication here, it means that data processing and computer people will be setting up their offices in the United States to serve companies in Canada. If that is not foolish, Madam Speaker, I do not know what is.
It seems to me that that kind of thing has not been looked at very closely. We seem to be hearing that that will be dealt with later. We have to think what transfer of information means today and what data flow is all about. It is communication across the country which has been built with a lot of subsidies and a lot of people saying "Yes, we want to build a country". We did it with the railway. We have done it with the airlines. We can do it with information flow with the technology of the 20th and 21st centuries but not if we give it all away which is what can happen with this agreement.
I heard that the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) had spoken to Conservative women a year ago saying that she wanted women to get involved in data processing and the new technology so that in 20 years from now they will be able to contribute as equal partners in the economic society. They will not be able to do that if we lose all our high technology data processing, a threat that is very real.
Before we implement this kind of an agreement, studies better be done. Will we lose control over our own information? We have so often allowed that to happen in the past. We allowed the Americans to go through our waters and we had to put up a Canadian flag to let them know that they belonged to us. Will we be in that kind of a situation when we transfer all our data flow and information north to south instead of east to west?
This morning I said that it was with great concern and lament that I rose to speak. My lament is that we are debating this matter in the House of Commons when Canada is looking at who it is and what its identity is. Abruptly we hear, "You better hurry up, Canada, if you want to retain that identity and you better get involved because the Government will not

November 24, 1987
Supply
let you". The Government will give 10 seconds to people to present briefs. What about the final text, if it ever comes out while the hearings are on? We hear that it is delayed again.
How can any Government of this country treat its citizens with such condescension and such lack of respect? We have a history of saying that people are important, that we respect the dignity of individuals and groups, but we are no longer saying that. We are saying that the only thing important is multinational profits.
When you look at the briefs coming into the committee, Madam Speaker, and you see the kinds of people supporting free trade, it is clear that this Tory Reagan agreement will help the multinationals. There will be no respect for the dignity of the worker, the culture and the social futures of our country.
The things that we care about and that we have been able to build collectively have been very precious to us. When we criticize the agreement we also have to say what are we going to do. Some people have asked whether we are going to stay with the status quo. 1 do not think anyone has said that the status quo is what we want. If you look at the great free market, what happens is ad hoc short-term business decisions. There is no ability for long-term planning. We have seen what France and Sweden have been able to do. Canada itself can get into some-long term planning with diversification of trade. Canada will never do that if we tie ourselves to only one goal and only one trading partner, that of the U.S.
It seems to me that we are on the edge of some great opportunity. Let us not blow it. Let us go ahead with the kind of vision and future of our country that our 120 years history has given us. Let us not change direction now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be taking part in the debate later on and will refute a number of assertions which the Hon. Member has made in her speech. I want to congratulate her and thank her for bringing this motion to the floor of the House of Commons. We are finding that the more the facts are laid on the table, presented and explained to the people, the more they understand and support the agreement. We thank the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) very much for the opportunity given us today in the House of Commons.
In 1945 the average tariff rates were 45 per cent. The average tariff rates today are 9 per cent. There has been a liberalized trade movement going on for quite some time. In that period of time, have we become less Canadian or have we become more Canadian? Have we become a weaker country or have we become more proud of our country and stronger because of that? Has prosperity followed the reduction of tariffs or has poverty set in with the result that our country is going to hell in a hand basket as some of the socialists would have us believe? I ask that of the Hon. Member because the trade agreement is following a pattern that has been going on for years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Not so.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: You don't know your own Bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: In the last 40 years that these tariffs have been coming down, what is the Member's vision of Canada in that period of time? Why is she so afraid of the future?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the Member for the question. It is very important that we clarify the information coming out.
Certainly tariff rates have been reduced. We have had a better country for it and we have had better exchange for it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: You are a free trader.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Therefore, I think we would like to continue doing that instead of what is in this very foolish agreement. We have said that we will allow the countervails to continue and allow the non-tariff barriers to be there. We also say that we want the U.S. to decide with its laws how we will trade with them. That makes us much less Canadian.
We need to start looking at what we do well, plan and take a direction that is positive that can make Canada second to none in the world. I have great confidence in Canada and in Canadian workers. We do not have to give our country away to trade with others. The Hon. Member will recognize that the reduction of the tariffs has been something with which GATT has agreed, as well as the United States and Canada. We know the fishing complaint against Canada was lodged by the United States. The decision against our fish processing came out in the last week and that is something that was caused by the Americans complaining about Canada, because we were able to compete so well.
This agreement has not changed anything. The countervails can still exist. There is no dispute mechanism. There is a phoney five-person board set up to advise-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Be honest.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I am being honest and I am really upset that the Government would even put before the Canadian people the claim that that is a dispute settlement mechanism. There is no dispute settlement mechanism in the agreement. We have really just asked the Americans what they want. We have said, "Uncle Ronnie, I guess what you really want is all our energy, so come and get it. Maybe you would like to buy a little more than you have been able to buy in the past so come on in and buy it all".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Be sensible, Marion. You are being absolutely untruthful.
November 24, 1987

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I am not, I am being very honest. That is not untrue. The Hon. Member would know that if he read the overview I read. I like handing it out to people in my office because the Conservative package is the best propaganda package for people to read. When people read it, they say, "They wouldn't dare do that to us," and I say, "Yes, they did it to you. They are trying very hard to do it to you".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to address one of the areas of the motion that I believe is a statement in which all Canadians believe. We heard government Members saying that they want a full debate and all kinds of consultation. We know that in fact they are ramming this thing through by travelling only to provincial capitals.
I know the Hon. Member also represents Hamilton and I am sure she would agree with me that in Canada's industrial heartland, in Red Deer and in Estevan, the people deserve to have a say. I would like to see the trade committee come to Hamilton to hear firsthand what happened to the workers at Firestone.
The Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) has been railing and ranting. The fact is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is setting his timetable and the Canadian agenda because he wants to have his picture taken with the President of the United States on January 2.
Does the Hon. Member not think that it is outrageous that the Canadian people who live in places other than capitals of provinces will not have a chance to participate in this debate? I am not referring only to the effect of the trade agreement on women or to the continental energy plan. In particular, if the Government really wants a debate, why is it trying to ram it through before January 2 just so that the Prime Minister can have his picture taken with the President?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for her question. It is so true that the area of the country we represent is a highly industrialized area. If one reads only what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and government Members have been saying, one would think that the people there all support the agreement. There have been all sorts of recommendations made to stop this agreement quickly because the workers are feeling-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: How about the steelworkers' union?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The steelworkers are saying that they do not want to be a part of this. The Firestone workers know what it is like to have decisions made outside Canada when 1,300 jobs are involved.
Government Members are talking about participation in a major new direction for Canada. However, what is really happening is that government Members are dropping off for a day here and day there waving the Tory flag and saying: "You have just participated, now I will take this down to Washington and plant it there". It seems as though government Members are terrified to hear from the Canadian people
Supply
because they know that our roots are deep, our culture is strong and we are sick and tired of getting sold out.
I hear that the committee even has to travel on an inefficient aeroplane. The Government does not think it is even worth it to give committee members decent transportation. Government Members want to say that the committee flew across the country, listened to certain groups for 10 seconds and that is the end of it. That makes a real farce of citizen participation. It makes a real farce of them saying that they have any sense of what is happening and of how Canadians feel.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) began her speech by speaking of the Macdonald Commission. She praised the Macdonald Commission and said that it advocated jobs for Canadians. That is correct, it did advocate jobs for Canadians, but it also advocated very strongly a free trade initiative with the Americans.
Donald Macdonald who headed the commission is one of the greatest proponents and supporters of this initiative. He knows what is going on in Canada. He went across Canada and studied the situation and established the needs of Canadians.
That remark of the Hon. Member is in itself contradictory. The Hon. Member comes from the central part of Canada. We westerners have faced unfair tariffs because we have not had an agreement that would deal with things like the shakes and shingles situation. Those very Members with whom the Hon. Member is sitting waved goodbye when we ran into the problem of an unfair tariff on shakes and shingles. It was NDP and Liberal Members who said that we could not resolve the problem.
When the agreement was signed, the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) dealt with this very issue in a way that is satisfactory to the industry. If an agreement had been in place to deal with this situation, there would not have been that unfair tariff on shakes and shingles. This has been clearly stated by the industry.
Would the Hon. Member tear up the agreement if she was put into a position by her Party to do so?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. Obviously he does not know that the countervail on shakes and shingles still exists. Countervails can be put against any other industry as well. This agreement does not protect us from that.
I did not compliment the Macdonald Commission. I stated for a fact that the Macdonald Commission spent $10 million travelling across the country looking at the economy and consistently heard that the first priority was jobs. It commissioned 72 research papers and not one of those papers dealt with the service industry.
The Hon. Member should do his homework if he wants to ask those kinds of questions. This issue is too deep for us to be

November 24, 1987
Supply
superficial about it. I think it is important that we get a sense of it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: No, we have not seen it. Could I tear up the air? The final-

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in keeping with this debate, I am also the Minister responsible for the status of women.
Let me begin by saying that I am very interested in the fact that the Hon. Member made a 20-minute speech and did not refer to women very much. She spoke a lot about consultation. Let us just put this to bed. There was no consultation on the Auto Pact, there was no consultation on the Tokyo Round, there was no consultation on the Kennedy Round whatsoever. The Macdonald Commission did a lot of work on free trade which is part of-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: What are women saying about it?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I will get to that because it is really important. I will talk about women and I will talk about opportunities for all Canadian men and women. This Party and the women of Canada believe in opportunity. That is something in which the NDP does not believe.
This agreement is designed to prepare Canada for the next century, to ensure that our industries can grow from their Canadian base, to encourage new investment in world-scale Canadian enterprise, including Canadian investment as well as foreign, to create a framework for co-operative relations between Canada and our most important trading partner and to set up a bilateral precedent for further multilateral trade negotiations. That is good for women.

Recognition of the fact that trade between Canada and the U.S. should be governed by a set of regulations, not by politics, is the cornerstone of this Agreement. A joint Canada-U.S. committee that will act as a compulsory court of appeal in settling trade disputes, and a commitment to negotiating new trade legislation over the next five years should provide adequate assurances for investors and business people in both countries until the end of this century and throughout the next.
Although the Agreement acknowledges a certain form of economic interdependance, it respects our social and political differences. From the outset, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) defined a set of important principles as guidelines for the agreement. Our political sovereignty, our network of social programs, our efforts to deal with regional disparity, our
distinct cultural identity and our specific linguistic character, which together make up the very essence of this country, would not be negotiable.
Those commitments were made by the Prime Minister before the talks started, and they were met. The conclusions of the Agreement show that despite the unfounded fears of some of its opponents who maintained that free trade would be a threat to institutions and programs that help define our Canadian identity, none of these programs was ever on the table for discussion or changes prior to reaching an agreement on free trade.
[DOT] (M40)
[English)
Since the agreement was signed the Opposition has subjected Canadians to all sorts of conflicting myths concerning what the agreement is all about. It is only 11:40 a.m. and we have heard all sorts of that this morning. We have been hearing alarmist talk about the devastating impact on ordinary Canadians, women in particular. That is absolute nonsense and 1 am going to set the record straight.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Canada is a trading nation, has been since before it was founded, and fully 80 per cent of all our exports go to our neighbour to the south. Part of this growth in trade with the Americans took place while the Party opposite was trying to expand our multilateral trade. With not much success, I might add. We are continuing to pursue that option.
Hundreds of thousands of women's jobs directly or indirectly depend upon our access to the U.S. market. Secure and permanent access will mean increased opportunity for economic growth in Canada and additional jobs. That is what we talk about. Jobs for Canadian women as well as men. Our productivity will rise because of increased economies of scale since we will have unimpeded access to a market of 270 million people. Wages should also rise under that scenario. It has always happened when there has been an expansion of trading opportunities, and women will benefit from increased earnings.
Let me go into one particular myth coming from the Province of Ontario. That Government released a study entitled "The Free Trade Agreement and Women". A day before that study was released one of the Toronto dailies ran a front-page story saying that the Ontario report predicted 100,000 women would lose their jobs because of free trade. That is pretty scary stuff, I agree. It is also incorrect. One should take the time to look at what that report says and how the conclusion was reached. We have examined it pretty closely and the study does not support the conclusion. Remember when you took high school geometry and you had to have a conclusion. This report goes from hypothesis to conclusion with nothing in between.
The report did not say that 100,000 women would lose their jobs because of free trade. It said 100,000 women were
November 24, 1987

employed in Ontario manufacturing industries which are sensitive to a reduction in tariff barriers. The study focuses on footwear, textiles and clothing because they have high tariff protection. Right! What it does not say is that tariffs are not being dropped against low-wage countries which are the main source of import competition for Canadian firms. That is very important because our competition comes from offshore suppliers rather than the U.S.
It does not state, vis-a-vis the U.S., that Canadian producers have been holding their own, expanding sales in the U.S., and are looking for more opportunities to do so. It does not say that the Ontario study was based on a one-time rather than phased-in removal of tariff barriers.

No mention is made of the fact that another report, prepared at that time for the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women by Katie Macmillan of the C.D. Howe Institute, reached conclusions that were the exact opposite: Female workers, especially in the services industries, will see a major increase in job opportunities as result of free trade-the kinds of manufacturing jobs that are threatened by free trade are those that have been known for some time as offering the lowest salaries, difficult working conditions and very limited career opportunities.

The Ontario study also does not say that the textile industry, those who make the investment and employ these people, is very confident in its ability to compete given the phase-in period.
Let me just say that women tend to feel disadvantaged in labour markets. Not just in Canada but in most places. They are very concerned with possible adjustments arising from free trade. However, there are two kinds of adjustment. Let us deal with the first, because our Government takes women and their concerns very seriously and we have a record second to none in that respect.
Unlike the former Government, which did put labour adjustment in the Auto Pact and there is no question about that, although it had nothing else, we already have programs in place to help workers make the necessary adjustment, whether it be through language training, skills upgrading, or whatever. There is a transitional period of 10 years in many industries to allow businesses and workers to make the necessary adjustment.
The second kind of adjustment is opportunity, and that is a major outcome of free trade and something the NDP never mentions. Most women who may be affected will likely move to equivalent or better jobs in those industries which will be expanding because of free trade. Free trade will provide new opportunities for women rather than locking them into low-paying work ghettos.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)

speechtext:
The Opposition never thought these jobs were so great before. They used to talk about the same kind of thing, the low-paying job ghettos. I am concerned that trying to preserve the status quo in certain industries will merely preserve those low-paying work ghetto jobs. It is short-sighted and serves to shield women from the potential benefits of economic growth by burying them in occupations where their incomes will continue to lag behind those of men. The best thing that can happen to women is prosperity, growth and opportunity. What they are talking about over there is not my idea of equality and progress.
Many critics of the agreement have failed to recognize that there will be strong growth in the service sector. The Hon. Member gave us her whole misery piece on the service sector. Let me just tell her what some people in the service industry are saying. These are not big multinational corporations, these are local Canadian businesses. Chris Gee, President of the Canadian Association of Management Consultant said, "I'm very, very excited. With our world class expertise and our Canadian structures, I think it can have a blockbuster impact on our clients and our profession."
Sandra Besserer, Vice-President-that is a woman, by the way-of the Machinery and Equipment Manufacturers Association of Canada said, "Our members were complaining-" these are her words, not mine, "-like hell about the problem of service people crossing the border." That will be corrected with free trade.

Raymond Lafontaine, President of LGS, a computer and office automation consulting firm, said: "The Agreement in principle on free trade is a positive one. It will make it easier for Canadians in the services industry to work in United States. . .

Forget about all us politicians in the little hothouse we run here in Ottawa. Canadian men and women out there doing the work see this as the key to the future of their industry and their employees, many of whom are women.
The service sector has been the most rapidly-growing sector in the Canadian economy, creating eight of 10 new jobs over the past 10 years. This sector will continue to create opportunity for the employment of women in a wide range of jobs demanding a variety of skills. Many women are now employed not only in the retail and personal services industry but also in telecommunications, health, computer services, and financial services.
In 1986 Canada's service sector accounted for 76 per cent of all employment. That is a phenomenal increase. At the end of World War II it was 40 per cent. This is an exciting opportunity for Canada and Canadians because all indicators point to the continued growth of this sector in Canada as in other

November 24, 1987
Supply
developed and developing countries. However, Canada has a good lead.
Services growth, particularly commercial, tradable services, are expected to outpace growth in the goods-producing sector. A free trade agreement is expected to accentuate the service sector growth thus increasing job opportunities, particularly for women who make up more than half the labour force in that industry.

Flexible working conditions in teaching, retail sales and the health industry are particularly attractive to women who are re-entering the labour marker or who are trying to strike the right balance between a career and their family commitments.
The number of women on the labour market has increased 42 percent between 1976 and 1984, while most of the new jobs created were in the service sector. Women now make up 43 percent of Canada's labour force. Their labour market entry rate is one of the highest in the world, and there is every indication this trend will continue.

The average salary for women in the services industry is higher than it is in the manufacturing industry. Therefore, those jobs will be good for women. Do not forget either that women now own one-third of Canada's small businesses. They could not do that under an NDP government. This figure represents a 100 per cent increase over the past 10 years. Not only are the numbers increasing, but the success rate of women, as could only be expected, is almost twice that of men.
Simply put, women are half the talent and half the human resources of this country. It makes economic sense for them to be able to utilize their economic capacity and to have choices and opportunities. When women do not receive a fair return on their labour they do not participate equally in all sectors of society and all of us, men as well as women, are losers. There is no room for that in the Canada which we envisage for the future.
Yes, we do need training to take advantage of those opportunities. We need education and training systems and we are providing them to expand the occupation and career options of women. The Canadian Job Strategy is the first program which provides non-traditional help and skill enhancement to ensure that women have not only keyboard skills for the service industry but have accounting and management training so that they can turn those keyboard skills into something else. There are, of course, women in low paying jobs. The Government will ensure, as it has from the beginning, that they are looked after.
All Canadians, men and women, are ready to face the 1990s and the new century. Every time a key is turned in the door of a new home or in a factory that confidence is shown. Every time a kid passes an exam, goes into a post-graduate course, or takes an apprenticeship course, and every time a young couple gets married, Canada is helped and we become more confident
in our future and reflect that confidence. Every time a new family chooses Canada as its home that confidence grows.
As a country our future is what we make it. We want to create the opportunities, co-operation, and regional development that is so important to us as a nation. It makes me so angry that the two opposition Parties always treat women as though they are down-trodden and victims. Women are contributors to this country.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: They are participants and contributors and must have an equal opportunity to contribute to our future development as well as to share in our prosperity. It is to Canada's benefit that they succeed. I respect their ability to do so and I will help those who cannot.

Madam Speaker, in her remarks the Minister accused the Opposition of putting on the floor in this debate conflicting myths, I believe that is the term she used. I would like her to explain some of the conflicting myths put forward by Ministers and government Members in this debate.
On October 5, in a speech to the Export Association of Canada, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that we would have massive retraining programs because of the job losses resulting from this agreement. The next day in the House the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) said that there would be no new retraining programs as a result of this deal.
The following day the Minister of Employment and Immigration said outside the House that there was a potential loss of 500,000 jobs as a result of this agreement. That was recorded by the press but when he came into the House the next day he refused to explain his remarks made outside the House. As a matter of fact, he said there would be no job losses as a result of this agreement and that we could wait until January 1, 1989 to do anything about it.
In fact, in this debate Ministers have said all kinds of things with regard to job losses and job gains. They have been all over the lot. I would like the Minister to explain that conflicting testimony and evidence put forward to the Canadian people and to this House on this subject. Who is right?
The Minister has dismissed out of hand studies raised by the Opposition. Rather she is asking us to take a leap of faith in favour of this agreement, or to engage in wishful thinking of the jobs that will be created, what impact studies does the Minister have which she can put on the table for everyone to see to show that there will be job increases and in what sectors?
She does not have such a study. No one has produced it so far. The Government is proposing the agreement and the burden is on the Government to bring such a study forward but it has not done so.
November 24, 1987

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that there would be massive adjustments if necessary, but no one expects there to be a need for massive adjustments. Let us get the facts on the table.
We have in place right now programs such as the Canadian Jobs Strategy which will provide adjustment, regardless of what the source of the need for adjustment may be. In this country there have always been series of economic changes which our economy has absorbed very well. That was shown in the Royal Bank study which came out only this week.
The Hon. Member asks for studies. I quoted from the Katie Macmillan report which talks about women. All the third-party, independent studies which have been done by people in the business community who deal with this kind of thing all the time have all talked about an increase in jobs in Canada as a result of this agreement. That is what we are basing our certainty on.
All the trade agreements which have been signed in modern society have led to an increase in jobs. Countries have ended up better off as a result of trading agreements. Agreements have been reached between groups in Africa, South and Central America, and between New Zealand and Australia. They are better off as a result of trade. I am not saying that they will be perfectly even over time, but if you compare where they started and where they are today you will see that they are better off now.
With regard to the European Economic Community, someone pointed out the other day that they have had more economic problems in the last couple of years than have we. It is partly because this Government has created a good economic environment in Canada. If one considers that agreement back in the 1960s and 1970s, they have done extraordinary well.
It does not mean that free trade is a panacea, but it does mean that there will be opportunities and growth in the future as a result of this agreement. It will be beneficial to people in this country, particularly women.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, will the Minister comment on the current debate in the United States as expressed in the newspaper U.S.A. Today's. On November 5, that paper devoted a full editorial page to the debate in the United States as to whether there ought to be compulsory unpaid maternity leave granted to companies with 15 employees or more. The great opposition to this comes from the United States Chamber of Commerce, which is the most vocal opponent to the family and medical leave bill being proposed in the United States House of Representatives. The bill would only require firms of 15 or more employees to give new parents up to 18 weeks unpaid leave with the guarantee of a job on return.
The Chamber of Commerce predicted economic catastrophe if the bill is passed. They also expressed their view in this
Supply
paper that maternity leave is only one of a number of many different alternative types of benefits that could be offered to employees, including pension coverage, dental benefits, flex time, health insurance and so on. They went on to discuss how companies could face competition in the domestic or international field.
I raise this question because we are talking about the Government's suggestion that we should really integrate our economies. In view of the Neanderthal attitudes that exist in the United States with respect to these issues, and our approach in Canada toward legal protection and programs to protect women and other workers, does the Minister of State not recognize that the atmosphere created by this agreement will result in intense pressure on this country against advancing the rights of women in the workplace?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member's statement about integrating our economies absolutely takes my breath away. The fact is that no other trade agreement in the history of the entire universe has integrated economies. Let us get it straight. This is a trade agreement, it is not an economic union or a political union.
Two years ago Members opposite said that our social programs were on the table and would be eliminated. We have an agreement and our social programs are not eliminated. It is certainly not our credibility that is at stake in predicting the future because we made a commitment to our social programs today and our ability to have social programs in the future.
The Opposition seems to frequently overlook the fact that in order to have the type of social and regional programs, in which, I am sure, the Hon. Member has some interest, we need additional prosperity. We must look ahead in order to determine how we will grow, not only in order to afford the kind of programs we have now but the kind of programs we would like to have in the future. That will only occur in a growing Canada that is creating jobs and wealth, and spreading that wealth a little better than we have in the past, which is another major objective of the Government.
This agreement will not only help women in southern Ontario, it will help women across Canada, including those in the Hon. Member's riding in Newfoundland.
Those are the very important considerations for us: First, that we create more jobs; second, that we create more capital; and third, that we invest that capital into more job creation in Canada and the kinds of social programs that this country has come to expect of this Government.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Madam Speaker, the resolution before the House asks us to consider three aspects of this free trade agreement, the first being the impact of this particular free trade agreement on jobs, particularly jobs held by women. Second, we are asked to consider the impact of the agreement on our energy resources and our ability to control our own energy resources. Third, the resolution states that the process by which we are

November 24, 1987
Supply
dealing with this free trade agreement fails to allow for adequate consultation with Canadians in all provinces and territories before committing us to profound changes, not only in our economy but in our political sovereignty, cultural distinctiveness and, generally, our ability to run our own affairs.
I want to deal with the third part of the resolution first. In all the 22 years I have spent in this Parliament I have never seen a measure so important as this dealt with in such a summary, cavalier or inadequate way. This free trade agreement will impact not only on every part of our economic life, including resources, agriculture, the Auto Pact, service industries, the food processing industries and so on, but will also impact on our social and political life.
The Hon. Minister who just spoke said that there is nothing in the agreement relating to social programs. That is correct. However, she does not say that because of this agreement there will be increasing pressure to harmonize social programs in Canada with social programs in the United States. Businessmen will say that they will not be able to compete with U.S. industries if we continue to have our unemployment insurance at a higher level than that in the United States. They will say that they are unable to compete with the United States because of our marketing boards, which give a fair deal to Canadian farmers. Canadian businessmen will continue to say that they will not be able to compete if we have a rich medicare program such as we have, and will probably propose user fees and such things.
It is true that social programs are not in the agreement. But the agreement has been set up in such a way that it develops pressure to harmonize and eliminate the social programs we already have.
Let us consider the example we have had in the House in the last couple of months. The pharmaceutical industries in this country were telling us that we either pass Bill C-22 or they would not increase their investment in Canada, do research and development in Canada or increase jobs in Canada. If such industries are trying to apply that pressure now, without the free trade agreement, how much stronger will that pressure be with the free trade deal?
When we propose measures that are in the interests of Canadians socially and politically, they will make the argument that if this has any cost they will not be able to compete with American companies that have free access to Canadian markets. There will be this pressure to harmonize these programs.
Let us consider the process to which I referred at the beginning of my remarks. We are being asked to deal with a measure that will impact on every part of our economic, social and political life. The agreement was signed on October 5 and we are being asked to dispose of it by December 18, when the House adjourns for Christmas. A committee has been set up to hold hearings in only one city of every Canadian province, with only eight witnesses a day.
Yesterday, in Vancouver when the Opposition made a motion to permit additional time to hear individuals who were in the room and wanted to raise their concerns, Government Members voted that down. They only want eight witnesses per day per province on this most important deal, and in only one city. In British Columbia it is just in Vancouver. We are not going into the interior, or to Vancouver Island. In Quebec the committee will just go to Montreal. There will be eight witnesses for all of the Province of Quebec. We are not going to Quebec City, or to Abitibi, to the Gaspe Peninsula or Lac-Saint-Jean where there are very strong interests and concerns about this agreement.
The process is a farce. The committee on unemployment insurance spent more than six months on that legislation. I remember we spent over a year on the proposed changes to the Crow's Nest Agreement. In the committee on freedom of information I spent nearly a year. Although those matters are important, they are not nearly as important as this proposed agreement, yet we are asked to deal with it in this very summary and quick fashion.
It is probably true that Government representatives will say that "before October 5 we had consultations for over a year with various people". Yes, they did that but it was mostly with business and mostly in secret. By the way, Madam Speaker, at that time the discussions were with respect to a free trade agreement in principle. We did not have any specific agreement before us and the negotiations which were carried on were carried on in secret. Perhaps that is necessary, but the fact is that the Canadian public was not involved in the debate.
Government representatives, when they stand up to answer, will probably say that this debate will not end on December 15, that in the new year, as a result of the signing of this agreement, there will be all sorts of legislation that will have to come before Parliament dealing with this matter and we will have a chance to debate that legislation. That is correct, there will be Bills to amend our Customs Tariff Act, our agricultural legislation, our transportation legislation, even the Post Office Act. There will be all kinds of Bills to amend legislation resulting from this free trade agreement, not only at the federal level but at the provincial level. The point is that it will be too late then to turn this whole matter back. I should not say it will be too late, but it will be very, very difficult to turn this around once they sign the agreement on January 2.
There will be Bills in the provincial legislatures and many Bills here in the federal Parliament. I suppose they will be dealt with in various committees, with one committee not quite sure what the other is doing, as is usual around here. One committee comes out with a report sometimes that is contrary to a report coming out of another committee, both prepared in good faith.
The point is that we should have more time to deal with this agreement right now before it is signed by the Prime Minister
November 24, 1987

(Mr. Mulroney). He is trying to meet a timetable laid down by the American authorities, its fast-track system. He is trying to meet that timetable when the impact of this agreement will be much higher in Canada than in the United States. Some estimates I have read indicate that only 10 per cent of American foreign trade is in Canada. Of our foreign trade, 60 per cent of it is with the United States.
The impact in this country will be much greater than in the United States, yet we will not even have the same amount of time in our Parliament and parliamentary committees to examine this deal as will the American Congress. For example, the American Congress will have 90 days to examine the agreement after the signing by the President and the Prime Minister on January 2. It will have 90 days, until April 1, yet our Government is asking us to complete our examination of this matter by December 15, after two weeks of committee hearings in Ottawa and two weeks of committee hearings on the road, with one day in each province.
We do not even have the legal text. All we have at this time is a 35 page text which is called "Elements of the Agreement". We are told that this 35 page "Elements of Agreement" text will grow to anywhere between 900 to 1,200 pages of legal text. The Government is asking Canadian unions, Canadian businesses, Canadian academics, experts and Parliamentarians, to examine these elements and make a decision without ever seeing the fine print, the legal terminology. That is completely unacceptable. That is not the sort of thing that is usually done in this country. It is not our tradition.
As a member of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade, in the short time we have dealt with this matter, each day with a new witness, I find that new insights are presented to us with respect to this agreement. Things no one has raised before are being raised by witnesses when they appear before us. That is what happens when we have a good debate. The more one looks at an agreement or a Bill, the more one understands it and sees implications one did not see before. When I read something for the second, third and fourth time, I see things I did not see before. Unfortunately, we are being cut off, not being allowed to give attention to this matter as we should, particularly since we do not have the legal text.
When the Prime Minister tabled these "Elements of Agreement"-35 pages-on October 5, he told us, and it also states right in the accord, that the legal text would be before us in three weeks. It has now been seven weeks and we still do not have the legal text. The Premiers of the provinces are meeting this week. They do not have the legal text either. I guess we will be left with one week or two weeks to look at a 1,200 or 1,000 page legal text and have to come up with a yes or no answer on whether it is a good or bad thing, even though it will touch on every aspect of our lives.
Some of the things being raised in a serious way are how the competition policy of the two countries will impact or be affected by this agreement, including the anti-trust policy and
Supply
policies relating to monopolistic practices. With this agreement more emphasis is placed on the so-called free market-place, but there are many experts who dispute whether the market is really a free one due to concentration, monopolistic practices, predatory pricing and all of those things. We have one type of competition law in the United States and another type of competition law in Canada, and one wonders whether we will have the ability to amend that competition law to prevent takeovers, concentration and actions by businesses to restrain trade, and not have fair prices. One wonders about all these things which have not been looked at at all.
I spoke about the process because I think the process is terrible. This is a complex, complicated matter. It has raised many concerns with Canadians. We do not have enough time to deal with it in a serious way.
I want to move now to the question of jobs, especially jobs that are held by women. As I tried to point out in my question to the Minister when she was in the House, we have had all kinds of estimates, studies and speculation on the jobs that might be lost or gained as a result of this agreement. The Economic Council first said there was a possible gain of 350,000 jobs, but that study was done before this agreement was made public. It was based on an assumed increase in productivity of 5 per cent per year as well as total access to the American market, including access to defence contracts. In the last few days we have had reports that the estimate of the Economic Council was way out of whack, especially when we look at this particular agreement.
There was a study done by Infometrica, released this week, which said the latest predictions contained in analysis prepared this week contradict previous forecasts of the Economic Council of Canada in a controversial study released in September.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: How many jobs does it say will be created now?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
It says 110,000, more or less. The point is that there have been studies on all sides of this question. There was a study done by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion which said that 228,000 jobs could be lost in 17 industries. There was a previous study done by Infometrica which said that 300,000 jobs could be lost. The auto parts industry has said it could lose 20,000 jobs. The wine industry has said it could lose 10,000 jobs. A study done by the City of Montreal said that 100,000 jobs could be lost in Montreal.
The fact is that because of these conflicting studies and no real serious impact study done by the Government, Canadians have very serious concerns. A Canadian who has a job now, and who has had a good job for 20 years, is concerned whether his job is in jeopardy. He is not satisfied by the rhetoric of the Government that there will be all kinds of new jobs. He does not know whether he will be able to adapt to a new job. If he or she is a person of 45 years or 50 years of age, will there be massive retraining programs? Will the individuals have to

November 24, 1987
Supply
move from the place where they lose their job to a place where the new job is located? There is no information on this.
I put it to the Government that it has the burden of proof. If it wishes to sell this deal it should have the studies and the specific information assuring Canadians that those new jobs will be there, what type of jobs there will be, and that there will be retraining and readjustment programs to relocate and readjust those people from the old jobs that they lose into the new jobs that might be there. The Government has not done that, so the concern of Canadians is justifiable.
Women are particularly vulnerable, because a very high percentage work in industries which are principally threatened by this deal, for example, textiles, footwear, clerical industry, service industry, food processing. When I speak about the service industries I mean telecommunications, travel, transportation, and so on, which can be done from the United States rather than Canada with deregulation and privatization.
To a very high degree, women work in those industries which are most threatened. In the textile and clothing industry 80 per cent of the employees are women. That industry is seriously threatened. For the first time in 15 years, last year the wage gap between men and women started to widen. It had been closing for 15 consecutive years, and now it is starting to widen again.
The Minister referred to the great Canadian Jobs Strategy. I wish to point out that, under the Canadian Jobs Strategy, women are unrepresented in the retraining programs right now. They have far from 50 per cent of the seats. They have a very low percentage of the seats.
The Canadian Jobs Strategy has been cut back in funding since 1984. In that year we were spending $2.2 billion on retraining and job creation. As of this year, that has been cut by 32 per cent from $2.2 billion to $1.6 billion. Yet the Government states that that type of program will be adequate if there is a massive loss of jobs as a result of free trade.
The other day the Minister and the Prime Minister pooh-poohed the study from Ontario which reported that 100,000 jobs in Ontario held by women were vulnerable or at risk as a result of this agreement. The report did not state that those jobs would be lost, but that they were at risk. That raises concern. The Minister's answer to that was that they are at risk, but they should have faith and believe in the Government. Why should they believe in the Government? Only 23 per cent of Canadians believe in the Government. The faith of Canadians in the Government has plummeted from 50 per cent in 1984 to 23 per cent across this country. The people do not have faith in the Government. It is up to the Government to put specific measures on the table to show that those jobs will not be lost. But, as I pointed out yesterday, if the jobs are lost the agreement should be changed with respect to food processing.
In the two minutes that I have remaining I wish to state that this debate is like everything else connected to the free trade deal. It is being rushed through without touching on many matters. I am sure that tomorrow I will receive calls asking why I did not deal with the impact of free trade on agriculture, the food industries, cultural industries, national sovereignty, the dispute mechanism, or on the Auto Pact. The reason is that we do not have time because it is being rushed through.

This is the most important economic, social, and political deal affecting Canada since the Second World War. It is being rushed through in an obscene manner.
This agreement gives the United States assured access to Canadian energy resources. I could quote the text, but the wording is contained in the "Elements of Agreement". More or less it will end the ability of any government to have any type of national energy policy in the future.

Even the type that Mr. Diefenbaker started back in the 1960s. The other day I attended a meeting with Mr. Lougheed, the former Premier of Alberta. I do not think that my hon. friend was listening to me closely. At no time in my speech did I state that our social programs would be considered unfair practices and, therefore, countervailable. I said with this agreement that our social programs will be at risk because there would be pressure to harmonize in Canada. I did not say that they would be considered as unfair trade practices. I said there would be pressure as a result of this agreement to harmonize. I tried to explain it in the following manner.
Since American companies will have free access to the Canadian market, Canadian companies will say that they have to compete with those American firms, they have to pay a higher minimum wage in Canada, and this makes it difficult for them to compete. Check-offs have to be paid for medicare and other social programs, and this makes it difficult to compete. In some provinces there are tougher environmental programs, and this makes it tougher to compete. What I am saying is that even though environmental programs, social programs, and marketing boards are not in the agreement, it is written in such a manner that it puts pressure on Canadian businesses to get rid of those programs in order that they will have the same basic costs as the American competitor who will come into the Canadian market.
