speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate that and I want to thank the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap). I was on my feet on debate, but I must admit that I have been asking a number of questions today and I can understand that Your Honour thought that I was still asking questions.
I am very pleased to participate in the debate today. Once again I want to thank the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) for bringing this motion forward, because it gives the Government yet another opportunity to present the facts regarding the agreement which has been reached between Canada and the United States that 1 most genuinely believe will be very good for Canada, for all regions of Canada. It will make us a stronger, more confident, more vibrant country than we are today.
We have heard many scare tactics today. It was kind of interesting to listen to the two opposition Members who spoke today. Neither of them offered an alternative to the status quo. They think the status quo is fine.
The first point which should be made is that there is no such thing as the status quo in trade today. Trade is changing rapidly. Protectionist moods are growing throughout the world. We must seize the opportunity presented to us to negotiate such a very important agreement.
I want to touch on a couple of things and then I will talk about consultation and the type of dialogue that has gone on regarding this agreement over the last number of years. I want to make one thing very clear. The Hon. Member said that the agreement will contain between 1,000 and 1,200 pages, but 800 of those pages are tariff schedules. They are not the text of the agreement per se. These tariff schedules must be appended to the agreement. Although it sounds awesome when you hear of an agreement made up of 1,000 to 1,200 pages, one must realize that 800 of those are tariff schedules.
The Hon. Member talked about how his Government consulted, negotiated and passed things. Let me quote him. I think the quote is accurate. "I came to the House in 1965 and the Auto Pact was already passed". The Auto Pact never passed anything. It was negotiated entirely in secret. It was
Supply
announced that it had been signed and it was a fait accompli. There was no motion in the House and no referral to a committee. There was not one thing. There was not one bit of consultation with Canadians on the matter at all.
I might point out that the people who opposed the Auto Pact in 1965, my friends in the New Democratic Party, were extremely vocal at that time, and their arguments used 22 years ago are the same arguments they are using today about the present trade agreement. Today the New Democrats are protecting the Auto Pact with their lives. They were wrong 22 years ago and I believe they are wrong today. Twenty years from now, if they are still around, they will be standing up defending this agreement as one of the most progressive and forward looking agreements that has ever been negotiated on behalf of Canada and Canadians. The New Democrats will be defending this agreement 20 years from now just like they defend the Auto Pact.
The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) talked about his Government reducing tariffs over a number of years from 1945 to 1984. That is correct. Tariffs did come down. They came down from some 40 per cent to 9 per cent over that period of time through GATT negotiations, the Kennedy Round, the Tokyo Round and so on. As the tariffs have dropped, prosperity followed. When trade barriers drop, prosperity follows. We have seen it time and time again; for example, in the European Economic Community. I am not afraid of tariff reductions and I do not think Canadians should be afraid either because prosperity follows.
I want to ask the Hon. Member from Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East-although I do not expect an answer- where did the debates take place in the Kennedy Round when the Liberals reduced tariffs and signed the agreements with GATT? Did the Liberals bring those matters to the House, refer them to a standing committee to travel across the country and get opinions from Canadians? Did the Liberals do it with the Kennedy Round and the Tokyo Round? No, Madam Speaker, they did not. This is the first time there has been such extensive consultation on a trade agreement. History will prove me exactly right to this point. I will go through the consultative process that has taken place concerning this trade agreement.
The motion in part reads: "fails to allow for adequate consultation with Canadians". Let us examine the facts. First, the previous Liberal Government put together a Royal Commission on the economy. Its job was to look to the future-not just tomorrow, not just to the next election-and determine what direction Canada should be taking to ensure prosperity, increase job opportunities for our young people and to ensure that we maintain our standard and quality of life. One of the major recommendations of that commission was a free trade agreement with our largest trading partner, the United States. I think everyone in this House will admit that there were very capable and prominent people represented from all walks of life on that commission. They spent a

November 24, 1987
Supply
tremendous amount of time and the taxpayers' dollars consulting with Canadians for three years, I believe. That was the recommendation from that commission.
Following that there was the Special Joint Committee on Canada's External Relations that travelled across the country. I must say it was co-chaired by my hon. friend, the now Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Flockin). Its recommendation at that time was to enter into a comprehensive free trade agreement with the United States. There were dissenting opinions. The NDP did not agree with it, naturally, but the New Democrats do not agree with anything the Government does. The Liberals said that they would like to talk about it and that it might not be a bad idea. The Senate committee looked into this matter and made recommendations. That committee spent time consulting with Canadians recommending that we enter into a free trade agreement. Independent studies from the C. D. Howe Institute, the Economic Council of Canada, the Fraser Institute and so on all recommended that we enter into negotiations.
When we got that kind of input from Canadians over a three year period, our Government decided to look into the matter and enter negotiations. The United States and Canada agreed to enter negotiations under the fast-track provisions of the U.S. trade legislation. That schedule has been known for two and a half years now. So it is no surprise, but the Opposition makes it sound as though it is something new and different.
What did our Government do? We set up an unprecedented program of consultation with the people of Canada. I can assure you, had the Liberals set up a consultation program with the people of Canada on the National Energy Program alone, and had they listened to Canadians, the National Energy Program may never have been created, but the Liberals did not consult Canadians. The NEP was a the brainchild of a few bureaucrats, Mr. Lalonde and a few others, without consultation.
Our Government wanted to make sure that Canadians participated in the trade negotiations. From the beginning we have had a two-way dialogue with business, labour, consumers and the provinces. The core of the consultation system has been the International Trade Advisory Committee which has provided a two-way flow of information between the Government and the private sector.
Under the distinguished chairmanship of a very old friend of mine, Walter Light, former chairman and chief executive officer of Northern Telecom-a large portion of which is in my community-the Government brought together more than 40 leaders from business, labour, consumer groups and academia. ITAC, the International Trade Advisory Committee, concerned itself with broad matters relating to international trade access and marketing. It has made valuable recommendations regarding the free trade association negotiating process. Under the ITAC umbrella we had 15 sectoral advisory groups on international trade, SAGITS. SAGITS represent a broad cross-section of the Canadian economy.
I want to read into the record today, with your permission, Madam Speaker, the sectors represented because it is most important that Canadians understand the consultative process which is being attacked by the New Democratic Party in its motion today. The list includes agriculture, food and beverage, fish and fish products, minerals and metals, energy products and services, chemicals and petrochemicals, forest products, industrial, marine and rail equipment, automotive and aerospace, textiles, footwear and leather, apparel and fur, consumer and household products, communications, computer equipment and services, financial services, general services and arts and cultural industries.
All these sectoral advisory committees were selected in close co-operation and consultation with the various national trade groups, provincial Governments and labour. Both the ITAC and SAGITs provided invaluable support to the trade negotiation team. They were used as a sounding board as the negotiations took place. The negotiating team asked what certain negotiations would do to certain industries, what it could do and if the industries could compete. This process went on throughout and the SAGITs were kept informed while informing the Canadian Government.
As a matter of fact, 150 meetings of the SAGITs and their working groups were held over the last 18 months. We asked for advice, we got it and we listened to it.
Over and above the formal SAGIT consultations, there have been dozens of briefings and consultations by officials from the trade negotiations office with all segments of the private sector and with individuals interested in the negotiations.
Apart from consultations with the private sector, the Government undertook to work closely and co-operatively with the provinces. First Ministers were briefed and consulted regularly as the negotiations progressed. They received briefings with slide presentations on every detail of the agreement.
Typifying the co-operative spirit which this Government has fostered through the Meech Lake Accord and other federal-provincial co-operative endeavours, First Ministers were kept fully apprised of what was going on, both at First Ministers' meetings and through a detailed network of contacts at the senior official level.
In fact, since the negotiations began, there have been eight First Ministers' meetings at which the free trade agreement was the single agenda item, two First Ministers' conferences at which free trade was extensively discussed, 19 full-day meetings of the senior officials' forum, the continuing committee on trade negotiations and scores of working-group meetings on every subject of the free trade agreement.
No previous Government has involved the provinces so extensively in such a comprehensive process of consultation and information sharing. Even Premier Peterson has admitted
November 24, 1987

publicly many times that he greatly appreciates the consultative process this Government has put into place, not only on this subject but on all other subjects for which federal-provincial co-operation is so very important to ensuring that Canada continues to grow and prosper.
It is not just the private sector and the First Ministers who have debated this issue. We have had a number of debates in the House on free trade. I believe this is the fifth or sixth debate we have had on this matter. Of course, on March 16 there was a major debate on a motion and since then a number of opposition Party motions have been brought before the House. We have had a very thorough and, I believe, a very extensive debate on this matter.
Opposition Parties have a number of allotted days left. They can bring this issue forward each time. As a matter of fact, 1 welcome the opportunity to discuss this subject on the floor of the House of Commons as often as opposition Members wish. We really appreciate the opportunity to put the facts about the negotiations on the table.
Hon. Members have spoken of the standing committee which has held extensive hearings. It has worked very hard in Ottawa. Its work schedule is probably three times harder than that of a normal standing committee which is holding hearings. It has worked tremendously hard over more than two weeks, not only being briefed but listening to all kinds of representations from people from all walks of life. I think that representation has been very fair. It has not leaned toward the supporters of the agreement or toward those who oppose the agreement.
Committee members are now crossing Canada. They are going from one coast to the other meeting those who are interested in appearing before the committee to let their feelings be known. A committee on a free trade agreement has never before done this in the history of Canada.
For Hon. Members opposite, particularly those from the former governing Party, the Grits, to criticize us for our consultative process and to criticize the committee's timing is something I find to be absolutely amazing and somewhat hypocritical.
I am very excited about this agreement. I am excited about the opportunities it will provide. I am travelling around the country making speeches and holding question and answer periods. Last night I was in Brockville. On Sunday I was in Whitby, and I will be speaking to the textile association and the Canadian Automobile Association tomorrow. The more the people understand and learn about free trade and the more I talk to them about it, the more excited they get.
What I find to be the most fun is that it is the young people who are grabbing this opportunity and telling us how much they look forward to it. The other night on television I saw a young man who is going to university here in Ottawa, but is from Windsor. He took offence to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) saying that he could

not compete with the Americans. He said: "You are telling me that I cannot compete with those fellows across the border in Detroit? I am a lot better than they are, I can compete with them, no problem at all". Those are the ones who are excited, are grabbing this opportunity and are running with it.
Looking at the attitudes of some of the provinces toward this agreement, I am saddened that the premier of my province is opposing this agreement. The philosophy of the Liberal Party in Ontario was made obvious when Monte Kwinter said what is good for Ontario is good for Canada. That disappointed me because past Premiers of the Province of Ontario like Frost, Robarts and Davis had the attitude that what is good for Canada is good for Ontario. That was their philosophy. However, the David Peterson Government of Ontario says that what is good for Ontario is good for the rest of the country. That is not the way confederation works. That is not the way I want to see confederation working.
This agreement with the United States will offer untold opportunities. On Friday, we debated the fisheries and talked about the opportunities it will give to the fisheries. I see that my hon. friend from Egmont is here today. He brought that particular motion forward, and again I thank him for doing so. It allowed us to put the facts on the table. I plead with members of both opposition Parties to keep bringing these motions forward when oppositions days come along. We love debating them. We love putting the facts about the trade agreement before the House.
I could cite this agreement chapter and verse, as I am sure Hon. Members could appreciate, but with the limited time available to me I must stop now. I do wish to encourage opposition Members to maintain their tenacity and to continue to bring these motions forward so that we can discuss the facts and so that the Canadian public can be well and properly advised. The fearmongering of the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party will be found not to be based on fact, and this will be proven here and around Canada in the days to come.
Excellent speech! Excellent!

subsubtopic: LUBICON LAKE INDIAN BAND-RECOGNITION OF STRUGGLE FOR SOCIAL JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Interreligious Foundation for Community Organization in the United States is an ecumenical foundation committed exclusively to the support of community organizing. For 20 years its members have been fighting for peace and justice. In that time they have contributed over $15 million to politically progressive organizing projects in the U.S., Africa, the Caribbean and Central America. In early December their twentieth anniversary program will be held in New York City. Among those participating are Mr. Ramsey Clark, former U.S. Attorney-General; Bishop Desmond Tutu, Reverend Jessie Jackson, and Mr. Harry Belafonte.
At their awards banquet to honour 10 of the most outstanding organizations in the struggle for social justice the honourees will include the U.S. Farm Labor Organizing Committee, the National Union of South African Mine Workers, the Nicaragua Baptist Convention, and, Sir, the Lubicon Lake Indian Band from northern Alberta. The unresolved land claim of the Lubicon Band is one of the great shames of this country and will continue to attract the attention of the world until the Government of Canada and the Government of Alberta make a fair settlement of this claim a priority.

Mr. Speaker, once again there is good economic news for the Mulroney Government from Statistics Canada. The rate of family income has risen and poverty has declined for the second year in a row. Some 525,000 Canadians have risen above the poverty line. Since 1984 we have seen a substantial drop in the number of Canadians living under the poverty line. Average family income increased in real terms in 1986 for the second consecutive year. After adjustment for inflation, we are $471 or 1.9 per cent higher than in 1985, and 4.2 per cent higher than 1984.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) brought out his economic statement, the Opposition cried that over 100,000 Canadians would be out of work. Instead, more than 1 million Canadians now have jobs who did not have them before, and over 525,000 are better paid and above the poverty line.
The free trade agreement will further reduce the number of Canadians living below the poverty line by increasing the
number of jobs, increasing real incomes, and reducing consumer prices.

On November 5 Route Canada suddenly announced it was closing its terminals in Sydney and Stellarton, Nova Scotia, and Bathurst, New Brunswick. The employees in those terminals, who have worked most of their lives for CN, are eligible only for the legal minimum in severance pay despite anywhere from 15 to 46 years' seniority with that Crown corporation.
Families in these three hard-hit communities are paying the price of the Prime Minister's privatization policy. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) should pay the price if he thinks privatization is such a good idea for Canada. Fair compensation from the federal Government is the least Route Canada's employees deserve after the sudden and unjustified shut-down of these terminals.
The increasing number of lay-offs in the trucking industry clearly shows that privatization and deregulation are costing us jobs now. More jobs will be lost in the trucking industry if the unpopular Tory Government has its way and forces our Prime Minister's and Ronald Reagan's trade scam through Parliament.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA HERRING FISHERY-SEINE LICENCE FEES
BRITISH COLUMBIA HERRING FISHERY-SEINE LICENCE FEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the roe herring fishery in British Columbia needs some leadership from the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon). At present there are approximately 250 seine licences and over 1,300 gillnet licences in this fishery. In recent years the fishery has become a nightmare for many fishermen.
It is generally recognized that fish companies now own a considerable number of seine licences and the companies have advertised in newspapers to purchase or lease other licences held by people who no longer want to use them. The annual fee for a seine licence is $2,000. Bona fide fishermen who want to fish are forced into a bidding war for these licences. Last year a seine licence was priced at $50,000 and upwards. Some boat owners have leased several seine licences, in effect slashing the number of jobs in the fishery.
The United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union estimates that 400 jobs were lost last year and that up to 300 jobs may be lost this year. In March of this year the Minister said, as reported in the Vancouver Sun: "Those who benefit should be those who are directly involved in the industry, not the people who sit in a chair somewhere".
The Minister has now sat in his chair for nearly a year and the patience of concerned fishermen is running out. I urge the Minister to take corrective measures now.

subtopic: SIZE OF PAYMENT TO SASKATCHEWAN FARMERS
SIZE OF PAYMENT TO SASKATCHEWAN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Western Grain Stabilization Program assists producers when net income from grain and oilseed seeds falls below the average of the past five years. The Act was amended in February, 1985, to allow for interim payments so that farmers could have cash in their hands prior to spring seeding. A record interim payment of $705 million was made in April of this year.
Last Friday, the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) announced a further final payment of $693 million under the WGSA for 1986-87. This brings the total WGSA benefit paid out to $1.4 billion, including $759 million to Saskatchewan, the largest pay-out ever issued and 63 per cent higher than last year.
As the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool President, Garf Stevenson, said: "It is a very substantial payment and it is very much needed. The payment demonstrates the commitment by the Government to support agriculture".

Mr. Speaker, the Government's trade deal with the United States continues to unravel. Yesterday the Government of Ontario stated that it will not agree to the terms negotiated for its wine industry.
On Sunday the General Council of the Quebec Liberal Party refused to approve the agricultural terms of the deal. The council members know that the deal is so unpopular with rural Quebecers that supporting it is like "throwing oil on a fire".
November 24, 1987

Similarly, western Canadian farmers know full well that their marketing boards and supply management systems are at risk as processed food is imported, bypassing locally grown chickens, turkeys and eggs, for example.
They also see no stop to the continued U.S. drive for bigger shares in the international grain market despite this costing ever more in grain subsidies and ill will from countries such as Canada, which have much lower subsidy programs.
Does the Government really believe that statements such as "marketing boards remain in place' will mollify farmers as they see their markets swept away by heavily subsidized U.S. production? Guess again. Farmers do not like what they have been handed by the Government and they are making their objections heard.

speechtext:

speechtext:

Under the Canadian Jobs Strategy over $60 million is provided for labour training for those wishing to enter the labour force. Some 85 per cent of that was used by new immigrants in 1986 and 1987. The Secretary of State provides funding for language training for citizenship purposes. Immigrant non-working spouses not destined for the labour force can take advantage of these programs.

However, I noticed in a newspaper clipping last week that the Hon. Member who proposed this motion was at a meeting where they were talking about the Auto Pact. I am not sure that she completely understands how the Auto Pact will work under the free trade agreement because she did not point out at the meeting that the Canadian content remains at 60 per cent with the big three. She seemed to indicate to the audience that it would be 50 per cent North American for the big three as well. Will the Parliamentary Secretary clarify that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
1 thank the Hon. Member for his question because I know he comes from an area that is deeply concerned about the auto industry, as is my community of Brampton.
First, only the big three will belong to the Auto Pact, according to this agreement. Second, we maintain the safeguards which demand that for every car they sell in Canada they must build a car in Canada. Let me point out that at this time they are 186 per cent over that requirement.
The requirement of 60 per cent Canadian content under the Auto Pact remains in place. As a matter of fact, the Canadian content in automobiles being manufactured here under the Auto Pact is at 70 per cent or 71 per cent.
In addition, we have said that if those automobile companies from offshore that are manufacturing either in the United States or Canada want duty-free access across the board between our two countries, they must have 50 per cent North American content in automobiles. That 50 per cent North American requirement pertains to labour and materials. The 60 per cent Canadian content under the Auto Pact not only refers to that, but also to advertising costs and many other things to make up the 60 per cent Canadian content. On the other hand, the foreign auto manufacturers here and in the United States have a true 50 per cent North American content requirement.
Our auto parts manufacturers in Canada can compete and have proven that. They have increased their share of auto parts in North America from 9 per cent to 14 per cent. They will be able to compete even more in the North American market with the duty removed. We believe that will expand jobs in the auto parts industry.
I know that the auto parts companies with whom I have discussed this in my particular community heartily support the agreement and look forward to selling parts, not only to the big three but to those manufacturers from other countries that are assembling and building cars here.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, again I thank the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary for that answer. Could he explain why the American parts manufacturers seem to be opposing this deal?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is interesting to observe the various groups in the United States that are opposing the free trade agreement that has been reached between Canada and the United States. One of them is the auto parts manufacturers in the United States who are petitioning Congress not to pass the agreement because they believe Canada got the better of the deal. When 1 see that, together with the coalition of energy companies in the United States that are opposing the agreement because Canada got the better deal, I know that we are on the right track. I am absolutely positive of that when I see that the AFL and CIO said at their meeting in Miami that Canada got the better of the deal and will oppose the agreement in the United States.
It is interesting to note who is opposing this particular agreement and who is saying that Canada got the better of the deal. I believe we both got a good deal because it is a win-win situation. It will be important for both countries, but especially for Canada where it will create jobs and assure a better way of life in Canada by making stronger, more proud and more efficient Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to take part in this debate on some aspects of the arrangement between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the United States, which some people misrepresent as a free trade deal.
November 24, 1987

The motion by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) states:
That this House condemn the Government for its signing of a trade
agreement with the United States that, amongst other things:
(a)	fails to consider the disproportionate effect on women, and especially the loss of jobs in the service sector where women are concentrated;
(b)	will give up provincial control over energy resources in a continental energy market; and
(c)	fails to allow for adequate consultation with Canadians in all provinces and territories before committing us to profound changes not only in our economy, but our political sovereignty, cultural distinctiveness and generally, our ability to run our own affairs.
Since it is a very large subject, I wish to comment particularly on two aspects of it which have been referred to earlier today, especially by some Hon. Members opposite.
I represent Spadina, which has a vigorous apparel industry, sometimes referred to as the garment, clothing or fashion industry. I want to comment on some things that have been happening there, as well as on some thoughts that have occurred not only to the trade unionists but also to the manufacturers.
Previously, it appeared that this was one of the sectors that strongly supported what was supposed to be the deal worked out between Canada and the United States. However, I found last week and the week before that now that the facts are beginning to come out, the Government is losing some of its supporters. The most notable one is the very chairman of the Sectoral Advisory Group for International Trade for the garment industry, Mr. Peter Nygard. Mr. Nygard is one of the larger manufacturers of clothing in Canada and understandably chaired that SAGIT. He is furious with the results.
He has been quoted both privately and publicly as saying that when the preliminary trade deal was unveiled last month a provision for quotas on imported fabrics blatantly discriminates against Canadian apparel manufacturers. He makes the point that Canadian manufacturers will get a ceiling of 50 million square yards of cotton and synthetic material in finished apparel going to the United States, and imports of woollen goods will be restricted to six million square yards, about three million garments.
The point is that the Canadian garment industry has been successfully selling about $100 million worth of exports to the United States, based on the expertise worked out in places like Montreal, Toronto, Guelph, Winnipeg and Vancouver.
There are only about 10 effective Canadian textile mills. There are about 250 American textile mills. Many good fabrics come from offshore. The Canadian industry has been able to sell to the United States a combination of imported and North American fabrics with Canadian design and workmanship. The same fabrics are available to the American industry
Supply
but, nevertheless, Canada has been able to compete successfully. The effect of the free trade deal has been to face Canadian industrialists, the employers, with restrictions.
Mr. Nygard perceives that the Canadian manufacturers will lose 40 per cent to 50 per cent of the $100 million worth of garments now exported to the United States.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I hear the Hon. Member opposite saying it is nonsense. I am not surprised he says that because apparently there was an attempt to muzzle Mr. Nygard. He is reported as saying that he and Mr. Oscar Rajsky of the Forsyth Trading Company were urged by federal officials to back off criticisms of the pact. He said: "We were told it was not in our best interest to go public. They, the feds, held out hope that they could negotiate around a very awkward situation".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Read the quote by Rajsky where he denied that. Be honest.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I have what the Sun provided. I do not answer for the quality of the Sun's reportage. I have the article and it does not quote Reisman.
It is not only Peter Nygard who is very dissatisfied, but Mr. Chris Kuzik the executive director of the Toronto Dress and Sports Wear Manufacturers' Guild, both in private conversation and his brief last week to the Ontario Government, has indicated he is very dissatisfied with the deal between our Prime Minister and the President of the United States.
For example, on page 2 of his brief to the Ontario Government he points out that wages and benefits of the employees within the guild are 40 per cent higher than they are in the southern United States. In the past, as has been pointed out, the main threat of imports to our industry has come from very low wage countries outside North America. This Government followed the pattern of the previous Government in allowing such a large amount of imports that the Canadian share of the market was reduced from about 70 per cent to about 50 per cent in a few years. However, the effect of this deal, according to Mr. Kuzik, would be to reduce the Canadian share further. He agrees with Mr. Nygard that 50 per cent of Canadian production will be affected or restricted by the deal which has been negotiated.
Mr. Kuzik particularly points out that, yes, the SAGIT was consulted. Mr. Nygard and his associates were consulted. They gave their recommendations. But he says:
Through our SAGIT the industry recommended to the Canadian negotiators that given our relative small size and other difficulties, an asymmetric tariff phase out be negotiated. This calls for: the phase out of tariffs in textiles before apparel; the phase out of U.S. apparel tariffs before Canadian tariffs. This was not accomplished.
This is a very serious problem and what is expected, according to Mr. Kuzik in conversation, is that a good many of the small plants in small towns across the country will lose out as well as some of the new, young and imaginative designers in

November 24, 1987
Supply
Toronto. He is also concerned about problems of labour adjustment. He knows his workers. There are about a dozen thousand workers in the industry and, as usual, about four-fifths of them are women. He points out that they are generally of a higher than average age for industrial work, with limited formal education and usually a lack of proficiency in any of Canada's official languages. The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) referred to the defect in our language training programs as it regards housewives and many others who come in originally as spouses, even if they later enter the labour force.
Mr. Kuzik also adds that unfortunately there does not exist any general retraining capability in Ontario to assist the employees who will be affected. The federal Department of Manpower stopped supporting on-the-job training within companies and industry-wide training or retraining years ago. A major retraining school along Spadina Avenue in Toronto is long overdue. He further points out that in his observation, the adjustment is going to hurt a great many of the workers in the industry, and I quote:
The reality I deal with is that with a plant closure, most higher wage workers have to take reductions to secure alternative employment. Through personal experiences involving hundreds of workers over many years, trade adjustment means to me lower wages for higher wage unionized workers, the opposite of what economists promise with free trade.
He refers to the training program again:
In 1982, it was expanded to the Labour Adjustment Program, which last year helped about 5,700 clothing and textile workers generally over the age of 54 having a minimum of 10 years industry service. These workers, mostly women, were permitted to receive the equivalent of U.I.C. benefits until they reached age 65. This was a compassionate program-
He then points out that the program was cancelled August 17, 1986.
This brings me to points which have been made by one of the well known ethical teachers in our country, Bishop Remi De Roo. Several years ago he lead a group of Bishops of the Roman Catholic Church who made an important statement criticizing economic systems that generate unemployment, that is that they were going far beyond the "hand out" philosophy which some people imagined was the Christian approach to unemployment. He makes five specific ethical criticisms, that is, criticisms on the basis of the ethical teaching of the Roman Catholic Church. In conclusion he makes this point:
In the final analysis, what is required is an intensive national search for alternative economic strategies.
This morning we heard someone call for alternative ideas. That is what Bishop Remi De Roo is proposing. He continues:
To be certain, the world we live in today has become highly competitive. Yet, the options before us are not simply free trade or increased protectionism or trade wars. As an alternative, I believe we need to mount a more selfreliant, less export dependent economy, with planned and diversified trade initiatives, not only with the United States, but particularly with certain Third World countries who are striving to reorganize their own economies to serve the basic needs of their people.
The point that Bishop De Roo has made repeatedly is that the first concern of our economy and the first concern of the
economies of those Third World countries should be to serve the people of the country rather than being, as he calls it, export driven. The submission further states:
For Canada, this involves a national economic strategy that puts priority on achieving full employment, new investment priorities and incentives, revitalized universal programs, new forms of community ownership of industries, a revitalized public sector, and a progressive tax system.
In the few moments remaining, I wish to mention a few of the particulars which Bishop De Roo raised in his brief to the committee on free trade. One of the points that he has asked for is what he calls the recognition of the proper status of human labour. This applies specifically to the Roman Catholic Church but it is also agreed to by other churches. The submission states:
The Church's social teachings emphasize the value and dignity in God's plan for Creation-Human labour, therefore, should not be treated as a commodity to be bought and sold in the market place ... It is through the activity of work that people are able to exercise their creative spirit, utilize their human dignity and participate in the development of their society-human labour and the basic rights of working people should take priority over the maximization of profits and the accumulation of capital.
Bishop De Roo points out that this is the "priority of labour" principle.
What we are getting in the free trade deal is too narrow an emphasis on the operation only of the employers and the salesmen; too narrow an emphasis that tends to underestimate the problems that will be faced by workers in the transitions that may be forced by the trade deal.
Bishop De Roo reminds us that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) offered the prediction that half a million or more Canadians could lose their jobs. He also points out that in Quebec a study shows that 30,000 people in the textile industry alone are faced with potential job losses. Yet the federal Government's job creation program does not seem to be gearing up to take this into account.
As has been pointed out, not only by workers but also by manufacturers in Spadina, the Canadian Jobs Strategy does not take account of this type of restructuring. Too many of its programs are open only to someone who has been unemployed for six months or more.
The women and men who work in the garment industry are not wealthy enough to take a six-month holiday while they wait for retraining. From the Government's point of view, if they make the mistake of taking a job in between, then they disqualify themselves for the retraining program because they have broken their period of unemployment which the Government wishes them to maintain.
There are also certain industries in Canada which are likely to be extremely vulnerable. It is not only a few out-of-date buggy-whipped industries. For example, the Bishop suggests that forestry, textiles, clothing, leather and shoes, furniture, electrical products, food processing, automobiles, and services such as health care, day care, and services for the elderly are
November 24, 1987

vulnerable to the changes that will flow from the proposed trade deal.
We have already had some suggestions of these events. The trade deal does not so much convert a situation from absolutely one thing to another, as to speed up certain tendencies. We have already seen tendencies, for example, American corporations taking over services such as child care, hospital services, and applying standards that are very different from the standards that have been built up by Canadians; standards of service and protection of the client whether it be the children in the day care or the patients in the hospitals; standards of services that are seen as a restriction on the profits of those corporations that come in to take over a hospital or a day care system in certain parts of the country.
We know that if we maintain or advance legislation that restricts the profit by protecting the standard of service to the service receiver, we stand in danger of being told that that is an unfair restriction on trade because it prevents the United States, or the American corporations, from making as much profit as they would expect to make in Canadian industry.
Therefore, the Bishop is also very much concerned with the question of social equality. The U.S. corporations generally consider that many of Canada's social programs such as medicare and unemployment insurance are a burden on the industry. In previous negotiations they have called them "unfair subsidies". We can expect that attitude to resurge and grow more aggressive under the free trade deal.
There is also the matter of regional development subsidies to one region. One American Government showed 55 Canadian Government programs, not all federal, which it considered unfair subsidies, which we considered appropriate regional assistance. There is probably only one type of regional assistance which the American corporations would approve of, and that would be the manufacture of military equipment. It may be suggested that the solution for unemployment in many parts of Canada will be to become part of the branch plant system for the American war industry. That is not acceptable to the majority of Canadians.
We also have the problems that have been previously referred to in agriculture, and perhaps it could even threaten the resolution of native land claims.
Those are only a few of the points that have been made both by industrialists in Toronto concerning the industry that they know intimately, and by Bishop Remi De Roo, one of the leading Bishops of the Roman Catholic Church in Canada. 1 hope that Hon. Members opposite will take warning from the information that those people have brought to us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can say very seriously that a great deal of what the Hon. Member has stated today is totally unfounded and, in some instances, is totally unfair. I especially wish to mention the Peter Nygard situation.
Supply
If the Hon. Member were honest and fair, he would have mentioned that there was an accusation made in that particular newspaper article from which he quoted that people were pressured not to appear before the committee. Mr. Nygard was not available for comment because at the time he was in Barbados. The other gentleman mentioned in that article stated that there was absolutely no pressure from the Government at any time. That is contained in that same article. If the Hon. Member were fair in his presentation, he would have read that quote into Hansard.
We must understand why Mr. Nygard is upset with the agreement. The agreement states that garment makers in Canada cannot bring in material from offshore, make it into clothes, and then ship it into the United States. There is a limit as to how much can be brought in from offshore, manufactured into garments, and shipped into the United States.
What we are doing here is helping the Canadian textile companies. If the Hon. Member is saying that what should happen in this agreement is that there should be unfettered access by the textile manufacturing companies around the world to Canada to manufacture clothes and then ship them to the United States duty free, and forget our textile manufacturers in Canada, then let him stand up and say so.
I might also remind the Hon. Member that the same holds true the other way. There are limits on American companies producing garments out of Third World material or fabric coming from other than the United States. It is a quid pro quo. The free trade agreement is not designed to be channeling things in from offshore, doing something with them, and then sending them down to the United States. That is not what it is about. I understand Mr. Nygard's concern. He would love to have unfettered availability of fabric from offshore; I understand that.
Once he understands what Mr. Nygard is concerned about, I think the Hon. Member, in all fairness, would have to admit that in the agreement we have protected textile purchasers in Canada and have allowed them to expand their operations, because they can compete very well with American textile operations.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: They cannot.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Many people in the textile industry say that they can. The Hon. Member was in the House this morning when I quoted all the people in the textile industry who say that they can compete. In any event, that is one point upon which I would like the Hon. Member to comment.
Also the Hon. Member keeps quoting Bishop Remi De Roo as a great tsar with knowledge of everything. He is the same bishop who said, in 1984 when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) brought in the economic direction of the Government of Canada, that hundreds of thousands of jobs would be lost.

November 24, 1987
Supply
He was the same one who said that the economic direction of the Government of Canada would lead us to disaster.
As everyone knows, over 1,000 jobs have been created per day since the Progressive Conservative Government was elected in 1984. Well over one million jobs have been created and over 570,000 people have been taken off the poverty roll. We admit that that is still not good enough, and we are working to get more off the poverty roll.
Bishop De Roo was wrong on that one, and Bishop De Roo is wrong on this one as well.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 wish to comment on the remarks that the Hon. Member made. I was referring to Nygard's statement as recorded in The Star. I was also referring to the fact that he had made an earlier public statement in objection to the free trade deal with the United States. I was not referring to the question of whether they were appearing before the committee.
I agree with the Hon. Member that Mr. Rajsky says in his story that his decision not to appear before the committee did not have to do with that pressure. I am referring to previous statements in the general public sector, that are in public knowledge and that were referred to, particularly statements by Mr. Nygard printed in the daily papers.
As to Mr. Nygard's reasons and the possible argument that the Hon. Member has used to set his reasons aside, that is the sort of thing that ought to be brought out for public decision or public examination before things are settled rather than after things are settled and signed. There are many things to be said on that, and it is not reasonable to choose to accommodate certain American industrialists and perhaps certain Canadian industrialists, the much smaller number or the tiny fraction of Canadian industrialists that might benefit, without public examination and consultation.
As for the Hon. Member's dissatisfaction with Bishop Remi De Roo, Bishop De Roo is held in high regard in many parts of Canada. He does not happen to be from central Canada. Perhaps that is why the Hon. Member from Brampton does not like him. He happens to be from the West and in many matters he reflects the point of view of the West.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I didn't say I didn't like him.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I am sure the Hon. Member does not dislike him personally. He just dislikes what he knows of him, that is all. It is interesting that it is a voice from the West that the Hon. Member from Brampton is trying to put down in this manner.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to add a comment to the speech which was made by the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap). Earlier today in the House it has been said-and it was not by the Hon. Member for Spadina but I invite him to comment on it-that Canadian textile mills were just as able to compete with mills elsewhere.
I would like to put the following information before the Hon. Member for Spadina. Recently I received a letter from a mill in my constituency which employs 72 people, most of whom are women, and pays an average salary of $ 11 per hour. They may not be very high wages, but in the case of the textile industry they are relatively high compared with what some other employees are making as salaries working in that industry. All things being equal, the wages are not as low as they are in other textile mills. Nevertheless, the letter is from the Texturon mill, a smaller textile mill, and it reads as follows:
This letter is written objecting to the planned agreement on free trade with the U.S.A.
You are familiar with our operation on Cameron Street in Hawkesbury at which we produce textured polyester yarn in a modern plant with excellent high-speed equipment. Should total free trade with the U.S.A. be placed in effect, we beyond doubt will have to close our plant in Hawkesbury.
We could not possibly compete with firms in the U.S.A., one of which presently produces in excess of five million pounds weekly. Our production in Hawkesbury is approximately 200,000 pounds weekly.
The situation is that the plant in my riding produces a small amount compared with some very large U.S. plants. Indeed, some U.S. plants have so much excess capacity that by eliminating one coffee break they could probably produce more than the whole plant in my riding could produce in one day.
Does the Hon. Member agree with me when I say that the effect of free trade on situations like the one I have described in my constituency is indeed disastrous, and that it is not quite true to state, as has been stated earlier, that we can compete with textile mills in the United States?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for raising a point on the basis of very pertinent fact. I could only say, from the facts he has presented, that I think he has made his case very strongly. I would add that I think the management and owners of Dominion Textiles agree with him in a sense, since over several years they have been shutting down their plants in Canada and opening plants in the southern United States in order to get at the low-wage area in those anti-union states. Therefore it is clear, wherever the ownership of Dominion Textiles is, that they will prefer to shut down Canadian plants and to open American plants.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madame Speaker, the Opposition motion on the Free Trade Agreement was negative and reactionary. One of the first defenders of free trade, Sir Wilfrid Laurier-a Liberal-would have added that it was no more and no less, and I quote:
-then a direct and unworthy appeal to passion and prejudice.

No aspect of the free trade debate better reveals the differences between the Progressive Conservative Party and the Liberal-New Democratic alliance than the debate over the
November 24, 1987

energy aspects of the free trade agreement. It is in energy that the benefits we have achieved foreshadow the benefits we can expect from the broader trade agreement. It is in energy that I will recall that our record of success and co-operation stands in such stark relief to the bitter failures of previous Liberal-NDP policies. It is in energy policy that our different visions of Canada stand in clear contrast.

Since September 1984, we have rectified the previous Government's policies that had such a disastrous impact on the energy sector. We started by deregulating oil exports and went on to revamp the regulations on gas exports, and we are now looking at the changes that should be made in regulations for exporting electric power. Previously, we eliminated a number of arbitrary measures that were giving Canada a reputation for being against investment. And finally, we have improved our access to export markets.
Madam Speaker, did you know that as a result of the Conservative Government's policies, today more Canadians than ever before benefit from a wider range of energy products, thanks to a more competitive market? These same policies have made it possible to weather the ups and downs of oil prices by giving us access to an expanded North American market. We aimed for bigger markets and reinvested the resulting profits in exploration and development instead of leaving our resources untapped.
We have been working together with the provincial governments, making excellent progress in this respect, to analyze and understand the vital role of energy in Canada's economy, the importance of trade and especially the importance of energy security.
Most of these gains were possible as a result of changes in administrative policies and procedures on both sides of the border. The Free Trade Agreement will officially sanction these arrangements and provide additional assurances for exporters and importers, both in Canada and the United States.
The text of the motion before the House today condemns the Government for giving up "provincial control over energy resources in a continental energy market". This allegation, this accusation, unfounded though it is, is just a new way of formulating the same old alarmist cliches the Opposition has been mouthing since the beginning of this debate. I will list them one by one, concluding with the text of the motion itself.
The Opposition has said that we have undermined our sovereignty in reaching a free trade agreement with the United States. This is untrue, Madam Speaker. It also shows a misunderstanding of sovereignty. Sovereignty is the ability of each nation to formulate its own laws and develop its own policies. Entering a free trade agreement involves accepting
Supply
some constraint on our behaviour. We have both agreed to reduce, and eventually eliminate, tariffs, for example. We have both agreed to refer disputes to binding arbitration where applicable. Without these types of restrictions, an agreement will be meaningless for both our countries. It would not achieve freer trade.

In the Free Trade Agreement we have not relinquished our ability to formulate or implement an energy policy that benefits Canadians nor our responsibility for doing so. The provinces will continue to set and collect royalties. We will design tax systems and provide incentives that will ensure resource development that is commensurate with the needs of Canadians. We will continue to set criteria for protecting the environment. We will also go on reviewing proposed takeovers in the downstream sector of the oil and gas industry. Madam Speaker, thanks to the mechanism for settling disputes, we have expanded the framework of our sovereignty by establishing rules to protect both countries from arbitrary actions on the part of either country. Our energy market will be North America, but our energy policy will be Canadian. Yes, we will have an expanded energy market, not a continental energy policy. That is the fundamental distinction the Opposition fails to make in its motion.

Our energy market will be North America, but our energy policies will be Canadian. We will have a broadened energy market but not a continental energy policy. The Opposition seems incapable of making this simple distinction.
On the issue of investment, I am pleased the Opposition has already recognized that a free trade agreement will improve the investment climate in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The Hon. Member is very good in English.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
With the additional assurance of access to U.S. markets, investors from Canada and many other countries will find Canada a more attractive place to do business. This is a necessity in a world where the international flow of investment increasingly ignores international boundaries. However, we have not changed our policy of reviewing proposed acquisitions. We do continue to reject proposals to acquire control of healthy Canadian oil and gas companies. In this way, we have maintained the careful balance we have achieved over the past three years between improving the investment climate and protecting the Canadian character of the upstream oil and gas sector.

Madam Speaker, the Opposition claims that the Free Trade Agreement does not provide adequate protection against U.S. restrictive trade laws. That is false. Canada as well as the United States has safeguarded its rights, its ability to take

November 24, 1987
Supply
action against unfair trade practices. The Agreement guarantees appropriate and impartial settlement of disputes, in accordance with the laws of each country, and contains a commitment to harmonize legislation governing bilateral trade over a period of five years. Furthermore, and this is just as important for the energy sector, both parties have agreed on a consultation process to examine regulatory measures that might have an impact on trade in energy products.
The Opposition also claimed that the Agreement was not balanced because it required excessive and unacceptable concessions by Canada and we woud get hardly anything in return. A cursory glance at the Agreement and at what has transpired in the last three years tells us that the opposite is true. Canada is benefiting already and will benefit even more from free trade, especially in the energy sector.
Since September 1984, we have broadly deregulated our energy exports, and we have done so in our own interests, not as a favour to our clients. We deregulated because we learned a lesson from the economic disaster we inherited from the previous Liberal Government. We realized that the energy sector would have to be developed through decisions by the private sector, on a more open and more competitive international market, and not through intervention by a Government that would turn a blind eye to economic reality.

Let us not forget the extent to which Canada's welfare programs depend on our energy exports to the United States. In 1986, despite low prices, they accounted for 11 per cent of all our merchandise exports, putting $9.9 billion in the pockets of Canadians. These exports are at the core of regional economies from coast to coast, whether oil and gas in the West, electricity in British Columbia, Manitoba, Quebec and New Brunswick, or uranium from Saskatchewan and northern Ontario.
The free trade agreement eliminates existing tariff and nontariff barriers to this trade and will prevent new barriers in the future. For example, our petro-chemical industry is highly competitive by world standards. Its current exports are $1.77 billion a year, of which 57 per cent is exported to the United States. These producers now face tariffs ranging from about 12 per cent to 18 per cent on exports into the U.S., the world's largest petro-chemical market. Under the free trade agreement these tariffs will be phased out and petro-chemical producers have enthusiastically welcomed the agreement. In some other areas, our exports face significant potential threats. It is no secret that many U.S legislators are strong advocates of an oil-import levy of $5 or $10 per barrel. Should the U.S. ever adopt such a levy, Canada will have the right to be excluded from the levy and thus benefit from a huge windfall in higher prices for our oil exports.

Madam Speaker, the free trade agreement makes official the changes we had undertaken on this side of the border and in our own interest. In exchange we get guaranteed access to
the American market, unfettered by tariff or non-tariff barriers, and a dispute settlement mechanism.
We have agreed not to impose measures unfavourable to our American clients, while they agreed not to be unfair to Canadian suppliers, or vice versa.
Madam Speaker, may I add that American protectionist pressures are also very strong with respect to hydro power. The American coal industry lobby is generously financed by an association called the Ad Hoc Coalition on International Energy Trade. This association is leading an unrelenting campaign against Canadian hydro power exports and fully intends to torpedo the free trade agreement. Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the leader of the socialist party (Mr. Broadbent) might be interested in joining the coalition? Be that as it may, the agreement will shelter us from this kind of threats and secure our exports of electricity.
All this seems perfectly logical and reasonable to me. We gain ready access to the American market. For its part, the United States wants to be treated equitably like any good customer who relies on a long-term supplier.
But the distorsions and demagogy of the Opposition show that they simply want to confuse the issue, discredit a reasonable trade deal, and make it sound like a threat against our security and sovereignty, while in fact it is the other way around.
The problem with the Opposition is its view of energy security which remains rooted in the disastrous and discredited National Energy Program which sought independence from world oil markets through oil self-sufficiency by 1990 and with it the ability to pretend that the price of Canada's energy resources could be made in Canada. This proved to be a costly illusion in every way, in lost economic opportunities, in unnecessary divisiveness between regions, and in a tarnished reputation as a trading partner and as a good place to invest.
Energy security under the free trade agreement is an important concern of many Canadians. Let me reassure Canadians that the agreement will not imperil energy security. In fact, it will increase it.
First, let us recall the undertakings entered into under previous Liberal and NDP policies. Even former Liberal Governments showed some recognition that any energy security was an international problem that could not be resolved by retreat from reality. Even former Liberal Governments realized that we had some obligations to our allies and our trading partners.
In 1974, along with 15 other original members of the International Energy Agency, Canada signed the agreement on an international energy program which committed us "to take common, effective measures to meet oil-supply emergency by . .. allocating available oil among their countries on an
November 24, 1987

equitable basis". This remains an important obligation for Canada. Because we are one of the few IEA countries which is a significant oil producer, our international obligation could actually compel us to increase our oil exports in an emergency. The free trade agreement, by contrast, merely protects the United States' proportional share of our supply so that it would permit a decrease in exports in an emergency.
Let it be absolutely, unequivocally clear that Canada's IEA commitment entered into by a Liberal Government would be far more onerous in an oil emergency than the much more modest commitments in the free trade agreement. The Government remains committed to the international energy program because we recognize that Canada is a trading nation and our energy security is ultimately linked to the economic security of our trading partners.

Madam Speaker, let me add another sensible note to this debate. Thanks to the changes already made by this Government, including deregulation, Canadian energy products can now compete for a larger part of the American market. The Free Trade Agreement will make this official without radically changing the existing situation.
The changes related to the Canadian share of the American market with their advantages and disadvantages will take place gradually and occur when the economic conditions allow. We also have to remember that the Opposition has an outdated notion of energy security. It hides behind a rather dark past which goes back to a time when energy security meant Canadian prices for Canadian energy resources. Saying that this "Made in Canada" pricing policy failed miserably would be quite an understatement. The fact is that it cost Canadian taxpayers billions of dollars, alienated Western Canada, resulted in exhaustive bilateral trade regulations and cost billions of dollars in lost opportunities.
What the opposition fails to understand is that our supplies were not threatened in the past and that our markets have never been as well served as they are now. Our production and management capabilities are of international level. What we need is access to the market and this is what the Free Trade Agreement will provide.

It would run counter to everything this Government stands for to bring, with the free trade treaty, prosperity to Canada at the expense of provincial rights. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) put national reconciliation on our national agenda. This Government is the first to have signed a constitutional agreement with the full support of all provinces. I therefore find amusing the concern of the Hon. Member from the opposition Party that, through the free trade agreement, we could somehow have eroded the power of the provinces under the Constitution. Moreover, this agreement is about trade, not about jurisdictions or constitutional arrangements.
Supply

I have said many times that the rights and prerogatives of the provinces under the Constitution now are and will remain unchanged by the Free Trade Agreement. You will soon have an opportunity to read for yourself the final text of this Agreement and you will find that the fears of the Opposition are completely unfounded.
To conclude, Madam Speaker, I can say that free trade will not mean that Canada has to give up its energy future. On the contrary, it will assure this future. Every barrel of oil, every cubic foot of gas, every kilowatt-hour of electricity will be sold by the producers at the best price on the market. Whether or not this produces increased profits for Canadians will depend largely on the capability and attitudes of Canadian producers and distributors. I sincerely believe in their talents, their dynamism and their success.
Madam Speaker, contrary to the Opposition parties, the Progressive Conservative Party believes in the Canadian people. While the Liberals and the socialists would like to restrict our liberties and to hide behind the apocalyptic vision of a future market influenced by external contingencies, the Conservative Party puts its confidence in the people of this country.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister a question which applies in particular to the people of Alberta. I was there last weekend and I think there is a growing concern among people looking at this deal in greater detail and its implications down the line. As I understand it, this deal will bring in a continental energy policy to replace a Canadian or Albertan energy policy. It means Albertans will not be able to use their very abundant energy resources to establish a provincial energy reserve. If at some future time they should want or need to favour their own consumers, they will be unable to do so. They will be unable to promote the use of Alberta oil and gas for Alberta industries at reduced prices, for example, in the petrochemical industry. They are really losing flexibility in diversifying their economy which is so important to resource-based economies.
It seems to me that this is not only a continental energy policy that we need to be concerned about, but it is pretty obvious that this is the first step towards Canada losing its sovereignty.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if we want to have a reasoned debate on the free trade issue I believe we would be well advised to define once and for all, in legal terms so recognized on the international scene, just what is a continental energy policy. The day we do that we will then be in a position to know whether or not it is a continetal policy. No matter what he calls it, I would suggest we must define what is meant by a continental energy policy. There is no continental energy policy in the sense that the two governments have a common policy. If we had a continental energy policy we would have a common policy, we would have common tariff rates applicable to third parties, we would have only one tax system, we would have only one environment protection system, and so on and so forth, and this is quite false. Such is not reality. What we do have is access to a larger market. Canada will define its energy policies, just as it has done in the past. Nothing in the agreement throws environmental protection issues in doubt. Nothing in the agreement involves tax matters, regulatory decisions we want to impose, calculations we would seek to impose with respect to our surpluses. Nothing in the agreement puts a question mark on these issues. What the agreement does is to open an additionasl market for energy producers. The agreement provides that both parties agree not to tax exports
November 24, 1987

or raise that kind of barriers. What the agreement gives Canada is one additional market.
Madam Speaker, I should think that our colleague will admit there is a difference between a continantal market, if you want to put it that way, and a continental policy. It is not a continental policy. It is an additional market which Canadians are opening for themselves.
