Madam Speaker, now that we have that settled I would like to continue with my remarks. I want particularly to address one element of the motion that was moved by the New Democratic Party which deals with the effect of the Prime Minister's trade deal on employment opportunities for women.

November 24, 1987
Supply
As I am sure you know, Madam Speaker, my constituency is largely dependent on the textile industry. There are some
3,000	jobs in the textile industry and approximately 500 jobs in the footwear industry in my riding. A good number of those jobs are located around the Town of Hawkesbury, a very beautiful community which I invite you, Madam Speaker, and all other Hon. Members of this House to visit. When you go there you will notice all the textile factories that we have there.
These textile factories are threatened by the Prime Minister and his free trade deal. They are threatened by the agreement before us. Earlier today the Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) stated that Canadian textile mills are able to compete with their U.S. counterparts. That is easy to say, especially when it is not your job that is at stake.
However, the reality is that some of the plants in our country are much smaller than American plants. Many American plants are already working under capacity. If they want to increase their production they do not have to build new structures or spend new capital, all they need to do is to add a shift or a portion of a shift, and they can take away a lot of our business.
I would like to read a letter from which I read a few sentences earlier today. This letter is dated November 3, 1987, and is from Texturon Inc., a small factory in my riding. It has 72 employees, most of whom are women, and the salaries paid to workers there are in the order of $11 per hour. For a textile mill it is not bad. It is a lot better than some other textile mills which pay lesser salaries. However, many Canadians earn much higher salaries than that.
The letter is addressed to me and reads:
This letter is written objecting to the planned agreement on Free Trade with the U.S.A.
You are familiar with our operation on Cameron Street in Hawkesbury at which we produce textured polyester yarn in a modern plant with excellent high speed equipment. Should total Free Trade with the U.S.A. be placed in effect, we beyond doubt will have to close our plant in Hawkesbury. We could not possibly compete with firms in the U.S. A., one of which presently produces in excess of 5,000,000 pounds weekly. Our production in Hawkesbury is approximately 200,000 pounds weekly.
Many firms seemingly are taking the tactic of just going along with this Free Trade approach without seriously considering the consequences. Economists certainly predict a great gain for Canada over the long term but few are thinking about the businesses such as ours which will be forced to close.
The letter continues, saying that they have informed the union and their plant manager of a shutdown in the event that the Prime Minister's trade deal goes through.
This is a tangible example 50 miles from Parliament Hill, almost on our doorstep, of factories that will be shutting down as a result of the Prime Minister's ill-conceived, ill-though-out free trade deal.
In 1983, at a meeting in Sherbrooke, I believe, the person who is now our Prime Minister said to the people of Canada: "Don't talk to me about free trade. That issue was decided in 1911. Free trade is a danger to Canadian sovereignty. You will
hear none of it from me at election time or at any other time". Of course, that person is now the Member for Manicouagan, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). That is what he told Canadians. This conversion by the Prime Minister was provoked by a meeting he had with the President of the United States in Quebec City on March 17, 1985. Things have never been the same since that duet in Quebec City. I do not think the country has recovered.
The Prime Minister tells us that we need this trade deal for two reasons. First, we need a binding dispute settlement mechanism because, in his view, the Americans are using every tool in the book to prevent Canadians from shipping to the United States and selling our products there. He says that we need a binding dispute settlement mechanism so that in the future we will have a tailor-made mechanism to sort out the problem. That sounds good and I almost liked it.
The second reason that we need a free trade deal, according to the Prime Minister, is that we must guarantee our access to the United States. Therefore, we have guaranteed access and a binding dispute settlement mechanism.
The Premier of Ontario, the Hon. David Peterson, employed the services of a law firm, Blake, Cassels and Graydon, to do a study of the Prime Minister's free trade deal, particularly of the dispute settlement mechanism. The law firm studied four criteria of this dispute settlement mechanism and analysed how well it would work. The conclusion was that an application of these four criteria shows that the dispute settlement mechanism contained in the agreement is flawed in ways that are likely to result in a significant denial of Canadian access to the U.S. market.
In other words, according to this law firm's study, it will not work. Since the two main objectives of the Prime Minister have not been met, why do we have a free trade deal? The Prime Minister will have to answer that because we do not know.

Madam Speaker, I mentioned a while ago the number of jobs in the textile industry which exist in my riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. As you know, most employees in the textile industry are women. As a matter of fact, between 60 and 65 per cent of the workers employed in this industry are women and, as was mentioned earlier, the wages there are not very high. Some may say: If they are not really good jobs, why do you insist so much on keeping them? Madam Speaker, you are certainly aware that in a riding such as mine, where the unemployment rate can be as high as 10, 11, or even 12 per cent, such as in the Hawkesbury area, a low paying job is better than no job at all. Many of the women in these industries are single mothers and a great number of them hold positions which would make it difficult for them to be retrained for other jobs, if other jobs were available. As I have
November 24, 1987

already said, there are still many unemployed in the region I represent.
1 have here a Statistics Canada study based on the 1981 census. In this study published by the Ontario Women's Directorate, we find that the textile workers have yet another problem. The study mentions the level of education of the workers in the textile industry and in other industries which will be adversely affected by free trade. For instance, 25 per cent of leather and tannery workers did not reach grade 9.35 per cent have between nine and thirteen years of schooling without having graduated from high school and 12.3 per cent have an Ontario grade 13 diploma.
In the textile industry, 14 per cent of the workers have under nine years of schooling. In the clothing industry, 23.1 per cent of the workers did not reach the ninth grade. Free trade will therefore have a special impact on those who work in the clothing industry, and even in the textile industry as a whole. As I have just shown, Madam Speaker, this Free Trade Agreement will have particularly harmful effects on the workers of some of these industries, especially the textile industry.

There is a further problem with the textile industry. A number of the plants are in fact branch plants of U.S. corporations. The removal of tariffs will result in the export of jobs to the United States.

I am not saying that the benefit package offered to employees in the textile industry in Canada is great, but usually it is better than what is offered to people in similar industries in the United States and elsewhere. The second thing that will happen is that because of competition from the United States, some of our industries will have to further rationalize and change their operations and put more people out of work.

With all this evidence, one would think that the parliamentary committee would be travelling everywhere in this country to find out from the average Canadian just how he or she feels about this. But we will not have the benefit of that kind of process. The Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) think that the applause they hear from the cheering trained seals in the background in the Conservative benches means that the people of Canada approve of this trade deal. They do not. The Prime Minister cannot equate the cheering applause of Tory backbenchers with the consent and support of the people of Canada.
The committee travelled out West yesterday but spent only one day in the Province of British Columbia. That is most inadequate. The same committee will be spending one day in Montreal and everyone interested is supposed to participate. The committee will be one day in each province of our country. That is the kind of utter nonsense for which we hear applause from the trained seals opposite. Even if I were to believe the Prime Minister for one moment-which, of course, I do not-if it is that great and important, surely it deserves to be viewed by the people of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I read today an article in the Ottawa daily newspaper Le Droit with the following title: "Our love of Canada will protect us, says Wilson." The Minister of Finance is telling us to have confidence, and that this will save us and bring out the best in our economy and our country.
Madam Speaker, if the Minister of Finance and his Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) believe that that is all it takes to succeed in this country, I can tell you that they are neglecting their work and their duties as Ministers of the Crown. It is their duty to protect the interests of the Canadian people. It is the role of the Government. They received a mandate to do so. They were given a very large majority-unfortunately some would say, myself included-in the last elections. They were given the mandate of acting in the best interests of the Canadian people. They did not get a mandate to negociate a Free Trade Agreement. The Prime Minister could have received that mandate if he had so wished. But he did not want such a mandate. He told the Canadian people one year before the elections that he did not even want to hear about it. I quoted his words a short while ago.
As the Prime Minister did not want a mandate to negotiate such an agreement, I suggest that he now has no right to do so.

November 24, 1987

Two Prime Ministers before him have wanted a Free Trade Agreement, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mackenzie King. As I recall, Madam Speaker, both were defeated on this issue. I therefore invite the Prime Minister to also have the courage to go before the Canadian people with his agreement and to say: Here is what I have negotiated, do you want it or not?
For my part, Madam Speaker, I shall conclude by saying that the Canadian people will say no.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, what we as politicians say, 1 am sure, has a high degree of credibility in the country. However, on an issue like this, where opposing views are carried forward as they are, I believe that those who have studied the issue and those who have gone into it in great depth, are much more credible, and I refer to the report of the royal commission which was chaired by the Honourable Donald Macdonald. He says he stands behind the support for the dispute settlement mechanisms which will no longer be subject to arbitrary U.S. actions. Had this procedure been in place, the outcome of softwood lumber would have been completely opposite.
In May of 1986, when the shakes and shingles unfair tariff arose, the Opposition waved goodbye to this side of the House instead of looking for a solution with our largest trading partner. I would like the Hon. Member's comment on the position taken by this known Liberal supporter in the past, and I say "in the past" because I am sure the hon. gentleman, given the arguments made by the Liberal Party at this time, would certainly have to make a reassessment. I would like the Hon. Member's opinion of the position taken by this gentleman after a $20 million study which was commissioned by the Hon. Member's Party. I would like the Hon. Member's comment as to how he can take such an opposing position without giving consideration to Mr. Macdonald's statement? Taking into consideration that the area the Hon. Member represents has not been affected by unfair tariffs such as the tariffs on potash, softwood lumber, shakes and shingles, just to name a few, I would like his reason for taking such an adamant position and, really, what I feel is an irresponsible position.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is barely worth responding to, but let me try. First, the Hon. Member opposite says my riding has not been affected by some of the United States' unfair trade practices of the past. Need I remind the Hon. Member that the unfair countervailing duty placed against Canadian pork products affected the constituency I represent? The U.S. Farm Bill, with some $70 billion worth of subsidies designed to displace Canadian markets, I raised today in Question Period, and there has been a protest sent to the Americans via our Ambassador. That has affected the constituency that I represent. It has depressed the price of corn, for instance, in the province I represent and in the very riding I represent here in the House of Commons. So my
riding has been affected by the unfair trade practices of the United States.
It is certainly not true to say that the constituency of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell does not know what it is to have to negotiate with Americans and lose out on the deal because our Government is so weak-kneed. That point is totally wrong and I thought I should bring it to the Hon. Member's attention.
Second, the Hon. Member says that Donald Macdonald is in favour of free trade and therefore I should like it. That is interesting coming from the Hon. Member opposite. I can probably find someone who voted for or supported the Conservative Party, if there is anyone who still admits to doing that, who is against this free trade deal. Does that mean that every Hon. Member opposite should be against it as well? There is probably someone, a New Democrat, perhaps, who likes it. I do not know. I have not tried to find one. Mr. Macdonald is a prominent Canadian, and his position has been well exposed. It is not my fault that he is prominent. There is no equivalent prominent Tory. I will grant you, Madam Speaker, that that is a fact, and I know that. That type of jealousy of the fact that Mr. Macdonald is prominent should not be used by Conservatives across the way in the degree that it is used.
The Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain) states that I should not be using something that is not thoroughly researched, because I should respect people who have done research on this issue. Need I remind the House that I have consulted with my electors, and for me that is more important than any other means of researching any material.
I wish to remind the Hon. Member across that he too should talk to the people whom he represents. In so doing, perhaps he would be better informed not about what one group thinks, not about what the corporate elite thinks-as Tories often do-but about what the Canadian people, our constituents, think about the deal and what we should be doing.
If the Hon. Member wishes to use a well informed, reasoned document, I will give him the study by Blake, Cassels & Graydon done for the Premier of the Province of Ontario, a duly elected Premier, elected with a vast majority of support, winning most of the seats in the Province of Ontario and defeating the Conservative candidate who wanted free trade. He was elected on that mandate, and that is a powerful mandate.
I have that study in hand. I have quoted a few sentences from it concluding that the binding disputes settlement mechanism will not work at all. With those facts, surely the Hon. Member across would have to agree with me that there is good reason to question such a bad deal.
November 24, 1987

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) was close to tears earlier when he talked about the women whose jobs were at risk as a result of the U.S. Free Trade Agreement. I feel differently, Madam Speaker. Recently, I had dinner with the President of the Textile Manufacturers Association who told me that he was anxious for the Free Trade Agreement to be signed, because he was convinced that Canadians and Canadian Textile Manufacturers are quite competitive with their American counterparts. The problem is not with the Americans, but with the other countries of the world, and in view of the fact the Agreement is stricly between Canada and the United States, our companies will be in a position to grow and manufacture textile more cheaply. Then, we will be able to take on the huge European market, as well as the Japanese and others. That is right. Canadian businesses will grow and create new jobs for women working in the textile industry.
As far as the garment industry is concerned, Canada has not been competitive for several years. It is competitive with the United States but not with the other countries. It would be completely wrong to think that, following the signing of the Free Trade Agreement with the Americans, the number of jobs will decrease. Quite the contrary! It will increase, because the true competition we face in the textile industry is not with the Americans. Members of the New Democratic Party who made that suggestion this morning were wrong, and so was the Hon. Member who has just spoken. What is most unfortunate is that he is such a good actor, he was almost in tears crying when talking about the possible loss of jobs for women. Imagine that! Madam Speaker, he knows perfectly well that women are not going to lose their jobs. In fact, we are very likely to see that number increase in the textile industry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must say that I feel very strongly that this trade deal is perhaps one of the most critical issues facing Canada in this whole century.
When we discussed this inside our own caucus and Party, away from the audiences and the House of Commons, there has been deep depression. We honestly do feel that this is hitting at the very roots of Canadian sovereignty.
If the trade deal is carried to its conclusion, which is certainly what the Government intends to do, it will dramatically change the whole nature of Canada. Many of us conclude that by the year 2000 our economic and cultural ties will be north-south rather than east-west. Certainly, those of us on the West Coast know how strong that pull is already. With no means of protecting our economy, there is no question that this is the way that we will be going.
This deal is so serious that it seems that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) gave away the country because he was so anxious to reach an agreement and save political face.
Now Canadians and parliamentarians are being asked to agree to a pig in a poke. The public has not had an opportunity to learn about this deal. They have not received the basic facts, much less an idea of the significance of areas that are still pending, and I refer particularly to the seven-year provision for defining subsidies. This is a very ominous area that has many implications. There has been no final written legal text for the committee. The time frame under which we are all being asked to operate is absolutely ridiculous. Of course, now we have those one-day wonders, starting in my Province of British Columbia yesterday, which are a complete farce. In fact, they are an insult to the public and to Canadians who have the right to know about this deal and all its disastrous implications as far as their country and their jobs are concerned.
The Tories want us to trust them. A few minutes ago one of the Members was suggesting that we should leave this to people who have expertise in this area, have an act of faith and trust what the so-called experts are saying. The Prime Minister expects us to take a leap of faith and trust his Tory trade deal with the United States.
I would like to look at the record and remind Canadians once again how trustworthy the Government is, and how much we can bank on the statements made by the Prime Minister. Let me refer to 1983 when the Prime Minister was running for the leadership of the Progressive Conservative Party. At that time he referred to free trade and said, "We would be swamped. We have in many ways a branch plant economy in certain important sectors". He was certainly right. We agree

November 24, 1987
Supply
with him completely in that regard. Tie went on to say, "All that happened with that kind of concept is that the boys"-and I believe he was right there too-"would be cranking up their plants throughout the United States in bad times and shutting their entire branch plants in Canada. It is bad enough as it it".
Certainly I would be interested in hearing from my colleagues on the other side of the House their reaction to that statement by their Leader in 1983. Apparently he has now changed his opinion and thinks that there is nothing like so-called free trade to save us from a disastrous future.
Why should Canadians, with this kind of record, trust the Prime Minister and his negotiators and his Government in this deal? Why should we be asked to take the deal on blind faith without knowing all the facts or having a final deal and without the public having a chance to assess it?
We must remember that the Prime Minister promised an increase in old age pensions. Of course he tried to deindex them and would have done so if there had not been a massive protest by senior citizens across the country. This is the Prime Minister who said to us several times, "our universality is sacred", and then he deindexed the family allowance. This is the same Prime Minister who promised us fair tax reforms, yet the proposed reforms again benefit the wealthy and do not tax corporations fairly. He also promised us a national child care program, and we have been awaiting one for over two years. There is no question that Canadians have a right to be skeptical about the trade deal with the United States which the Government has been promoting.
Again I should like to summarize what this trade deal means for Canada. First, it was supposed to give Canadians free access to U.S. markets, but the U.S. still retains all its countervail laws-the countervail laws which apply to shakes and shingles, softwood, potash, et cetera. It was supposed to have a very strong dispute settlement mechanism, but the dispute mechanism is just a token appeal body which will uphold U.S. laws including entrenched countervail provisions.
Also it was to bring in a continental energy plan. It was interesting that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) did not like me using that term this afternoon. Everything we read in the American press related to this deal, and in the papers which we had before we even got the Canadian documents, indicated that that was what the Americans were calling it. At last they have their continental energy deal. It is worth anything to them to have that deal. Only Mexico was smart enough not to sign that kind of arrangement.
In 1983, the Prime Minister said that we had a branch plant economy at that time. There will be even more control by American parent companies over Canadian industries under this deal. There will also be open and U.S. investment in Canada. It is not difficult to imagine that pretty soon, as certain Canadian businesses or industries are bought up, or as
Americans start their own industries in Canada, we will again be the source of raw resources, and that manufacturing and the lucrative labour-intensive parts of these industries will be in the United States.
There will be a loss of jobs. Even the Government had to admit it. In fact, government Members have been very inconsistent about it, which shows just how little study they have done. One Minister has said that there would be a loss of
800.000	jobs. I believe another said that there would be a loss of 600,000 jobs. The original assessment of the Economic Council of Canada projected, if I recall correctly, that some
300.000	jobs would be lost, but it was not even considering the service sector. Now it wants the final documents so that an assessment can be made.
It seems only fair to Canadians that this deal should not be signed until we have that information. Surely Canadians have the right to know what will be the impact on their own jobs. There is no question that jobs will be lost in agriculture and in very sensitive manufacturing industries, particularly those in the West to which I will refer in a minute. Also there will be jobs lost in the service sector where 80 per cent of the jobs are held by women. Of course the Auto Pact and the parts manufacturing industry have been gutted.
If we add the Conservative policies of privatization and deregulation which were a lead-up to this deal, and then add on top of that the free trade deal, it is no wonder that Canadian trade unions are up in arms. The whole question of job security is threatened, particularly jobs at decent rates of pay.
I should like to comment on the implications for western provinces, particularly Alberta and British Columbia. We have really been concerned about the attempts in the House, particularly by the Prime Minister, to stir up a sort of regional racism. We are all committed to Canada. Let us look at the West, particularly the resource provinces of British Columbia and Alberta. I realize that all western provinces are resource provinces, but I am dealing now with these two provinces where there are highly sensitive manufacturing industries. Some Governments have been trying to bring in secondary industry. They always talk about it, but it is difficult to accomplish. However, at this point in time, western manufacturing industries employ about 70,000 people in food processing, metal, machine fabricating, furniture, textile, clothing, printing, and publishing. DRIE's studies show that there will be an extremely negative impact on these industries.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: That is the NDP talking.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
What about DRIE? Does that not mean something else to the Hon. Member? Jobs in new industries are also at risk. We know that three out of four western jobs are in the service industries which are beginning to build. We know that these will be hard hit. As well, our growing links with the Pacific Rim will be affected. We are just beginning, in British Columbia and also in Alberta, to enhance greatly
November 24, 1987

our relationship with the Pacific Rim with a view to establishing a much better trading relationship which is favourable to Canada. There is no question that it will take second place to a continental trade arrangement with the United States.
The trade deal is a threat to the Canadian way of life. The section dealing with seven years to define subsidies worries me especially. We know that the United States has always considered our Canadian social programs as subsidies. Although government Members keep saying that they are not included in the deal, if they are not included, why was it not stated explicitly in the agreement? As far as the seven-year definition of subsidies is concerned, social programs such as medicare, unemployment insurance, child care, and other human services are still very much there. In the view of many it means that regional development programs and cultural programs are on the table.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Just not true.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
There is nothing at all to say that this is not true.
Supposedly Canadian culture was protected, but as experts in the field have said, it is very narrowly defined. I would be interested in what the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) has to say on this matter.
I want to speak particularly about the impact of this deal on British Columbia. Even though the deal fails to reach the key objectives promised by the Prime Minister, B.C. has surrendered jobs in many key industries, our ability to expand and diversify our economy, and our autonomy to develop our own social and economic policies in the future. We particularly need to diversify our economy in the West.
The deal completely fails to resolve existing trade problems for B.C. industries. The export tax on softwood lumber is enshrined by the deal, while U.S. countervail duties on hogs and cedar shakes and shingles remain unscathed. Further, the deal offers no protection against future U.S. countervail duties on B.C. products.
In exchange, our manufacturing, farming, wine making-a new industry which has been making headway in British Columbia-and service sector industries are at great peril. We have surrendered any kind of effective control of U.S. investment in our resources or financial institutions, and we are compelled to share our energy resources with the United States.
Columnist Marjorie Nichols has noted, "What Canada has given away is its industrial future". Canada's chief competitive advantage among industrialized nations is our wealth of accessible energy supplies. Under the trade deal, the U.S. is guaranteed full access to these precious supplies at exactly the same price as they are available to Canadians. B.C.'s most precious asset is sacrificed and so is Alberta's. For what? A deal of so-called free trade that continues to allow U.S. protectionism against B.C. imports.
Supply
Former Premier Dave Barrett told reporters recently:
Complete resource access will leave us forever as hewers of wood and drawers of water. It's really an incredibly bad deal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Who are you quoting?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I hear snorts and sniffles across the House. The Member cannot sit and listen for five minutes without nattering. I hope he turns on a replay of the BCTV account of yesterday's hearings in British Columbia. He would have heard many groups saying that the whole process of hearings is a farce. The hearings are by invitation only. The public was not allowed to be heard. The TV cameras were not allowed to be present. There is an anti-free trade coalition comprised of 43 different groups, labour, church groups and community groups which, in effect, were given 20 seconds each to present their views through one presentation.
The shore workers and the workers in the fish plants-and I want to say that many are immigrant workers, many women working under difficult conditions, many from my riding-are very upset. Their spokesman said they were very upset at the GATT ruling which would disallow Canadian processing of raw fish which appears to be threatening some 4,000 jobs. They were upset because they are afraid that the free trade agreement, if signed, will bind Canada to the GATT ruling, a ruling initiated by the United States.
What about fruit and vegetables in British Columbia? The B.C. vegetable producers were given only three and a half minutes, an industry that will be destroyed in British Columbia. Consumers, I know, are sick and tired of having only imported fruit. The Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), I hope, will show some concern because it will affect some of the people, both growers and consumers, in his riding. There were also some very colourful statements, I might say, from Jack Munro of the IWA about the impact on woodworkers and their industry.
This is a bad deal, Mr. Speaker. There is no question about it. It is a threat to the Canadian way of life. I have mentioned subsidies, regional development and aspects of Canadian culture. We believe there is not enough proof that they are protected.
I would like to mention the impact from an Alberta point of view. I had the opportunity to be in Edmonton over the weekend meeting with people about free trade. I must say it was very educational because I learned a great deal. The Premier of Alberta and the past Premier of Alberta think this is a wonderful deal. As a matter of fact they think only wimps are opposed. I want to let you know, Mr. Speaker, that I joined the wimp protest meeting and I am proud of it. Under this deal the Premier and former Premier feel that Alberta will have nothing but benefits. I would like to ask, as I asked the Minister earlier, if this is a continental energy policy-which it is-

November 24, 1987
Supply

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Which it is not.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Alberta cannot use its abundant energy resources to establish provincial energy reserves if Alberta wanted to favour its own consumers if it wanted or needed to do so. Alberta cannot use Alberta gas at reduced prices for Alberta industries. I am thinking of the petro-chemicals in particular. Alberta will also lose its ability to process resources within the province. Processing resources is important to western provinces. We must diversify. We cannot be dependent only on non-renewable resources or we will have no future for our children.
This deal is definitely a first step toward losing our sovereignty. It prevents economic diversification in western provinces. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, I believe, said that the petro-chemical industry would really benefit because Alberta now has access to U.S. markets. I wonder how the Alberta petro-chemical companies, still subject to the U.S. countervail prices, can compete in the same way. They will not be able to continue to have a favourable price for gas, which has been important to them in the development of secondary industries.
Mr. Lougheed told the parliamentary committee that the deal is not only positive but it is a must for western Canada. I wonder how many Albertans who have studied this agreement would agree. Is it better to sell our resources for a quick buck today or is it better to try to have control over your own future and diversify your economy?
What about the farming sector, Mr. Speaker? Certainly in British Columbia the fruit and vegetable producers are very concerned. The wine industry is very much threatened. I know that in Alberta and British Columbia the red meat industry had great hopes for this deal, yet they did not get the access to the U.S. markets they had hoped for. We find also that the two price system for grain has been eliminated. Incidentally, the western grain transportation which goes through the Port of Vancouver to the U.S. and the two price system, I am told-I am not an expert in this field-mean a loss of some $300 million for farmers. It will be very hard for poultry and dairy farmers to compete.
In summary, this is a bad deal for Canada and for westerners. It fails to open access to key U.S. markets. It makes unwarranted concessions to U.S. demands. It undermines economic plans to diversify resource economies. It gives the U.S. guaranteed access to our resources at market prices. It opens the door for more U.S. takeovers. It leaves the door wide open to economic forces which we will not be able to control. It entrenches U.S. protectionist measures which will be very difficult for any future Government to change. It changes the very nature of Canada. About the only benefit that I can see in this deal is that it protects Canadian beer.
Bishop Remi De Roo said to the committee that this trade deal locks Canada into a multinational theology of the marketplace where people are things and can be discarded. My
Leader has said that the Mulroney trade deal is a betrayal of Canadian interests. It goes to the heart of our sovereignty as a nation. I agree with both comments.

-they are full of inaccuracies.
Let me start with the apparel industry. Everybody is talking about the apparel industry today-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade

speechtext:
-including the Hon. Member and about womens' jobs. Let us take a look at the facts and at what has happened in the apparel industry. Canadian exports into the United States of textiles-that is what Hon. Members from all opposition Parties are talking about today-have increased from $120 million in 1980 to $377 million in 1987. As a matter of fact, in the last two years, there has been an increase of over $100 million in exports to the United States. At the same time, imports coming from the United States have remained relatively stable. The market for Canada in the United States is growing. When the tariffs are removed, some of which are as high as 45 per cent, I might add, Canadians will be able to compete there very well. We only have one-third of 1 per cent of the market in the United States now. What a fabulous opportunity this will be for us.
Let us see what the Canadian Textiles Institute said, not at hearings in Ottawa but to the Ontario Government blue-ribbon panel. Its submission reads as follows:
The status quo was a bleak prospect. The best available alternative appeared to be a free trade arrangement with the United States although it was not risk free and would present textile companies with some formidable challenges. On the plus side we had been steadily improving our exports to the U.S. and had invested heavily in new technology.
The Canadian Textiles Institute has accepted the challenge. It is going ahead to expand its exports into the United States. Its submission went on:
November 24, 1987

-A growing number of firms favoured free trade. They saw the opportunities and benefits and were prepared to accept the risk in preference to the status quo.
A growing majority of firms believed they could survive in a North American free trade situation provided the adjustment and transition conditions were adequate.
Eric Barry, President of the Canadian Textiles Institute, said:
It is my personal opinion that the Canadian textile and clothing industries faced a brighter future within a free-trade arrangement than without.
The evidence is there. I have just mentioned the increase in exports of textiles to the United States. Once those tariff barriers come down, they will be able to go to the United States with no problem at all.
The problem with the NDP, and we heard about it from the Hon. Member, is that it is an inward-looking Party. It is myopic. It hides behind barriers, barriers to protect this little Canada. NDP Members have no faith in Canadians. They do not believe that Canadians are productive or can compete. They do not have any faith in the Canadian people at all. That is the difference between the dinosaurs in the New Democratic Party and the very progressive attitudes and policies this Government is taking.
We believe in Canadians. We believe in our ability to compete and in our entrepreneurship. We believe we have one of the finest educational systems in the world. We have a workforce that is far more productive now than the American workforce, and that has been proven time and time again.
The Vice-President of IBM told me the other night that the most productive plant IBM has in the world is in Bromont, Quebec. The number two most productive plant for IBM is in Don Mills, Ontario. Is that not interesting? Do not tell us that Canadians cannot compete.
The other day, I participated in an opening of a Computerland store. Computerland is the largest Canadian computer company in Canada. It ranks third out of 52 computer companies over all in Canada. I asked a representative of Computerland if he was afraid of the free trade agreement and if he thought it would knock him out of the box. He said: "Are you kidding? This gives us more opportunities than you can imagine. We are number three in Canada now, the number one Canadian-owned computer company, but we will soon be number one over all". There were probably about 800 people at that opening. When we talked about free trade, the house came down. They were all so enthusiastic about it and were looking forward to those challenges.
Why are members of the NDP so frightened of something that is so good for Canada? I will answer one of the Hon. Member's questions. She asked why social programs are not included in this agreement. It is because this is not a social document, it is a trade document. We are dealing with trade, not social policy. Social policy is totally outside this agreement and has absolutely nothing, zip, zero to do with this agreement.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the issue of free trade and to answer the Hon. Member's questions.
She said earlier that Canadians were not educated enough, that Canada was not rich enough, that Canadians were too cautious. That is more or less what she said.
Well, all I can say is that our country has enough human and natural resources to face up to the tremedous challenge of free trade.
If Canadians seem to be afraid of this great challenge, it is just because the Opposition is spreading a lot of false rumours about the Free Trade Agreement.
I am convinced that once Canadians have heard the truth about this great challenge of free trade, this grand design, the majority will support this plan, because I have met them several times in the course of my travels in recent weeks, and I can assure you that when you carefully explain what this great plan is all about, Canadians are willing to take up the challenge. Afraid? The two previous Governments stepped back from this challenge and it looks like they would have lost the

November 24, 1987
Supply
election if they had come before the House with this great plan for free trade with United States. Of course we knew this plan would be practically suicide on the part of the Government, because the Opposition would use it to spread a lot of false allegations and take the 5 or 10 percent of our industry that would be affected and make a mountain out of a molehill, and then load the dice against the 85 or 90 percent of our economy that would gain from this great plan.
That is why it takes a Government that has the guts to do it. We decided to follow through. And 1 can say that when we take the trouble to explain frankly what this free trade project will give Canadians, people are quick to understand and find the plan very acceptable. If this great free trade challenge was good for Ontario at the time of the Auto Pact, why wouldn't it be good for Quebec? Why wouldn't it also be good for Western Canada and Eastern Canada? After talking to a lot of entrepreneurs, I think 95 or even as much as 100 percent of the people I talked to, people who invest money in the private sector, agreed with me. How come the people who risk their capital agree with free trade and the people who don't are against it? I just don't understand, and it may be too late to find out why. But maybe we can answer the last question, and that is, why the people who risk their money are prepared to go along with the Agreement and those who do not are against the plan.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, l do not understand why the Conservatives keep on misinterpreting the Auto Pact. My understanding is that it was a negotiated settlement in one sector. It is not free trade. Yet the Conservatives continue to make them synonymous.
As to the statement that Canadians are not audacious enough, I think it is an insult for Members on that side to challenge the deep patriotic and personal feelings we on this side have for our country and fellow Canadians. Canadians have great capacity in many areas and we have proven this. We have built a very diversified country and achieved economic success. That is why we have a favourable trade balance right now. The evidence is that we are doing better than the U.S. Why do we need this trade deal? We do not have to give away our resources or allow U.S. takeovers. We do not have to entrench countervailing duties in our laws and we do not have to accept a threat to Canadian culture and social programs.
Why should we be doing those things in this trade deal? We are giving everything to the other side and we do not have to. We are doing very well in trade and we should proceed in an orderly way, sector by sector, where it is needed, in an international context.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this debate for several reasons. First, because it
provides me and the Government with an opportunity to tell Canadians about the importance of this very historic agreement and the benefits it will bring to the majority of Canadians. I for one will not pretend that the agreement will be well received by all Canadians or that it is good only for Canada and not for the U.S. If that were the case, there would be no agreement. However, I firmly believe this agreement is good for the majority of Canadians.
As I have sat here listening today I have been disappointed by the fact that the Opposition, both Parties, offer no alternatives when they address this subject. There seems to be a surprising, disappointing, and perhaps even naive assumption that somehow or other the maintenance of the status quo, without any effort whatsoever on our part, is in itself a policy. As you know, evidence of protectionism in many parts of the world, particularly in the U.S., is very much before us. We have to respond in one way or another and we believe very strongly that this is a positive response which will work to the benefit of the majority of Canadians. Quite frankly, we are afraid that what the opposition Parties advocate, which is essentially to do nothing, would in the long run mean the destruction of the Canadian economy as we know it today.
I am also struck by the fact that there seems to be so much criticism of this agreement from those who say it does not specifically address this or that and does not protect us from their fears, whatever they might be. As one who grew up on the Prairies I learned that there were two things we had to fear. One was drought and the other was grasshoppers. Naturally the free trade agreement does not protect us from either of those. They can occur in the future because, while they are very real threats to the western economy, they have nothing to do with trade. I suggest that many of the criticisms of this agreement have, by the same token, nothing to do with trade.
With respect to the motion before the House today, I want to say that I recognize the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) is sincere and serious in her efforts. I know she believes in the ideology and policy positions of her Party. For example, she believes that Canada must protect its sovereignty. We all believe that. Yet at the same time, she and her colleagues believe we should withdraw from NORAD and NATO. We should spend as little as possible on defence and the instruments we need to protect the sovereignty which is of concern to all Canadians.
As a good New Democrat, she believes we should keep interest rates as low as possible. Unfortunately, at the same time she believes that the Government should spend as much as it can and not worry about the size of the national debt or the budgetary deficits plaguing our country. It is those very same deficits which lead, of course, to the high interest rates that crippled our economy in years past.
As a good New Democrat, the Hon. Member believes we should not negotiate a comprehensive bilateral trade agreement with our largest trading partner, and that our interests
November 24, 1987

are best served in multilateral trade negotiations under GATT. That is what they have been telling us over and over for several weeks. Unfortunately, as a serious and sincere New Democrat, she and her colleagues also believe that we should refuse to accept any decision from GATT which does not agree entirely with Canadian policies or practices. The Hon. Member is serious and sincere but, in my opinion, seriously mistaken and misguided on this issue.
Is it any wonder, then, that the motion before us is such a mishmash of slogans and forebodings? Consider the NDP spawning ground. Never in the history of our country have we seen such a fertile source of contradiction and incoherence. They have failed to mount any effective criticism of the free trade agreement on economic grounds and are now unfortunately relying on the old slogans we have heard in Canada before. "You are selling out the country", they allege. "You are giving up our sovereignty". What a pathetic sight. What a desperate line of argument.
When the negotiations began, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said, and I think all of us remember this well, that: "Our political sovereignty, our system of social programs, our commitment to fight regional disparities, our unique cultural identity, our special linguistic character, these are the essence of Canada and these are not at issue in these negotiations". The fact is that the Government has honoured every one of those commitments. On culture we had Bill C-58, which is the principal economic support for our cultural industries and it remains intact. The special status of cultural investment in this country has been confirmed.
What about regional development? Our sovereign right to pursue initiatives in that area has been recognized. The western diversification fund is so important and so much appreciated in western Canada. The Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and the Northern Ontario Development Agency will all continue to assist those regions to diversify and develop their economy. Let us not forget who introduced these programs. It was this Government under this Prime Minister.
What about social policies which the Hon. Member spoke of? Medicare, unemployment insurance and all the other social policies to which all Canadians of all political stripes are committed remain intact. Furthermore, our sovereign right to meet the needs and wishes of Canadians is fully intact. In fact, we shall soon be exercising that sovereign right again when we introduce in the next few days, according to my understanding for the first time in the history of this country, a national day care policy. Is this the kind of policy initiative taken by a Government that wants to give up its sovereignty? No, of course not. This is the kind of initiative taken by a Government that knows how to exercise our national sovereignty in the interests of all Canadians.
Under the free trade agreement Canada is free to apply and introduce the economic, social, cultural and constitutional policies it chooses to introduce. That is exactly what we as a Government have done and what we will continue to do.
Supply
We undertook bilateral negotiations with the U.S. in the same spirit that we participate in the multilateral negotiations under GATT. Our objective is to make Canada's economy stronger and more internationally competitive through trade liberalization. If I may say so, I firmly believe that much of the prosperity we in the western world have enjoyed in the 40 years since World War II is a result of the trade liberalization policies we and others have agreed to.
We believe that a stronger, more competitive Canadian economy means a stronger, more independent sovereign Canada. The free trade agreement represents a new vision of Canada, a vision of a strong dynamic country with a leading role to play in the world. We see a bold, confident Canada in the future.
What is the vision of those who introduced the motion today and those who support it? In two words, it seems to me that that vision is one of myopia and insecurity. In my opinion, they regretfully see a smaller Canada, a Canada which seems to be threatened on all sides, and a Canada which is regretfully lacking in self-confidence. That is very tragic because I, as a western Canadian, understand very clearly that western Canada was peopled by those who arrived there perhaps some 100 years ago and believed in themselves, their region, and the potential of their region to become a very productive world trading community.
We have done that in the past because we believed in ourselves. We must have that type of vision going into the twenty-first century. Unfortunately, it seems that today there are all too many Canadians-and this, of course, is expressed most clearly by those in the opposition Parties-who lack that type of vision for the future. Instead, they have a disappointing and, I would suggest, incomplete vision of what this country can be.
Quoted in Maclean's recently, Paul Reichmann said, "Americans work hard. Canadians work better. We will prosper in a free trade deal".
We share this view because we believe it is a testimony to the confidence and faith of Canadians and in the ability, the drive, and the capacity to work hard which we have demonstrated in the past and which I believe we are anxious to continue in the future. We believe it is time that the Government of Canada demonstrated that it has the same faith in Canadians as Canadians have in this country and in their ability to perform and compete in the world community.
Unfortunately, not all Canadians share that view. It is evident from the motion before the House today that the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Mountain (Ms. Dewar) and her colleagues in the federal House, and I include as well some of their provincial colleagues in the Province of Manitoba, do not have that same faith in Canadians and in the future of this country. They seem to believe that the bigger government gets, the better it is. They seem to believe that Canadians must be

November 24, 1987
Supply
led by the nose by the bureaucracy and the state from the womb to the tomb.
However, I can say as a historian that history has taught us over and over again that the womb of the state is sometimes not unlike a tomb. What is meant to shelter often instead suffocates. History has also taught us that relying on the policies of the past to meet the challenges of the present is an approach which is often doomed to failure.
Curiously enough, today's critics of free trade harken back to the slogans and fear mongering of yesteryear at the turn of the century, the campaigns of 1891 and 1911. It is important that we not in any way confuse the patriotism of the past with what was, in many ways, a devotion to the British Empire. The issue today is not what was appropriate in 1891 or 1911, but what is needed in 1987, 1989, and into the 21st century.
Some have noted that the positions of Parties change with the passage of time. As an historian I remember very clearly the positions of the various political Parties in 1891 and 1911. However, it seems to me that what we must remember, what is often forgotten, is that the circumstances of the moment have changed as well. Those policies which were appropriate in 1891 or 1911 are not automatically appropriate in 1987 or 1997, as many in this House would have us believe.
I am very proud to be a Canadian. I say that as someone who was born in western Canada and received much of my education in western Canada but continued that education in the United States and lived outside my country for a while. I always knew I would come back to Canada. Quite frankly, I am pleased that I did, even though there have been, on occasion, economic reasons for remaining outside the country.
One of the reasons I ran for office some four years ago in a by-election is that I believe in this country, I believe in the potential of the country, and I believe in the people who reside in it. I believe in our values, I believe in our institutions, and I believe in what I think is our unique way of bringing fair solutions to the challenges we face as a country and a people.
I believe that we are very capable of responding to the challenges and, in this case, opportunities, to a greater extent than many people, and unfortunately even some Canadians, appreciate today. There may well be explanations which I am not party to, but I am disturbed by the fact that there are some Canadians today who seem to be losing confidence in themselves. There are some Canadians who seem to be losing confidence in the future. There are some Canadians today who are overcome by fear of the unknown, if you will.
In this agreement and the Government is asking Canadians to continue in our traditions of the past of having confidence in ourselves and of being willing to take some risks to try to develop the potential which is ours as we go into the future. As we do that, we must remember that we no longer live in an isolationist world. We no longer live as an island unto ourselves. We are very much a part of a global economy and depend very much on trade within that global economy.
My special interest, as you know, is agriculture. Some farmers have asked me on phone-in programs why we worry about trade, why we do not concentrate instead on the Canadian domestic market. We could do that, and I dare say there are some in the House who would advocate that, but it would be at an incredible price to ourselves.
As many of us who represent agricultural constituencies know, 50 per cent of agricultural income comes from exports. To give up that opportunity to trade, to say no to the opportunities which are before us in the free trade agreement and in the GATT, is to say no to our future, to say no to the 50 per cent of income which comes from exports and, quite frankly, to say no to the future of at least half of the Canadians who could no longer find employment in that industry.
In a global economy you either face the competition or you are out of competition. To be able to compete any industrialized country needs guaranteed access to at least 100 million people. Unfortunately, Canada and Australia do not have that guarantee within ourselves. Therefore, we look to a free trade agreement with the United States as a solution to that lack of guarantee. This free trade agreement will give us that guarantee, it will give us that market which is at least 10 times the size of the Canadian domestic market. It is vital to every sector of our economy; the resource industry, the manufacturing industry, and the service industry.
Canadian industry, large and small, has faced this fact. That is why virtually all industrial associations in this country, representing the large and the small, are now supporting the free trade agreement. They not only want to compete, they are begging for a chance to compete. These enterprising Canadians are committed to our unique social, economic, and cultural institutions. They know that these Canadian institutions can only be as strong as the Canadian economy. Of course, we are willing to pay a certain price to be Canadians, but we need the wealth which is generated by trade and we need the economic growth that results from trade in order to be in a position to do that.
Sovereignty is not something that is given to a nation. Sovereignty is something that a nation earns every day. For Canada, in my opinion, and in the opinion of the Government, trade is the key to that sovereignty.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciated the comments made by my hon. friend. They were thoughtful comments and, while I have some disagreement with a good deal of what he had to say, I appreciate that they were presented in the way in which they were.
I want to ask my hon. friend a couple of questions. Nearly 80 per cent of our trade is now with the United States. I do not think another country in the world has 80 per cent of its trade with one other country. If there are such countries, I am not aware of them. In the European Economic Community, for example, once a country is doing over 20 per cent of its trade with one the partners it begins to get very concerned and limits
November 24, 1987

any increase in trade with that country. They believe that 20 to 25 per cent is the maximum allowable because once it gets beyond that point the other country has a certain amount of control over your economy.
At this time 80 per cent of our trade is with the United States, and that is increasing in spite of some initiative over the last number of years to divert trade into other areas.
Would the Hon. Member like, as an ultimate goal, to have 95 per cent or all of our trade with the United States? How does the Member respond to questions which I and others on a recent parliamentary delegation to Singapore, the Philippines, Indonesia, and Hong Kong were asked at every stage? People in the business and international trading world were asking why Canada does not do more trade in that part of the world. They asked why Canadians do not aggressively pursue new trade options in their part of Asia.
There was a feeling that the amount of initiative in this north-south trade has been somewhat at the expense of pursuing aggressively trade in new areas, particularly the Pacific Rim in this case. I would like to hear my colleague's comments on both those issues.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, both questions are very appropriate and thoughtful. Canada is very much a product of its geography. Those of us who have taught Canadian history and have observed Canadian politics have sometimes said that indeed there is too much geography in Canada. There are many theories that Canada is one of the most difficult countries in the world to govern because of that geography. Without a doubt, the very presence of the Canadian Shield represents an immense barrier which the Government must very consciously work at to overcome. That geography has meant that we have developed more of a trade relationship with the United States as opposed to the relationship between countries in many other parts of the world where there are alternatives.
The Hon. Member mentioned Europe, where virtually any European country is surrounded by neighbours on two or three boundaries as opposed to the one boundary we have.
Smaller countries which have entered into the European Economic Community probably share some of the fears that I hear Canadians expressing today. For example, I hear people ask how a nation of 25 million can exist with a nation of 250 million. While that is a legitimate question, I suggest the answer first lies within our own country. That ratio has existed throughout our history and we are proud of the continuing peaceful relationship we have with the United States.
There are also examples in Europe where the very small countries are as comfortable with a free trade agreement as are the large countries. As a matter of fact, countries are
Supply
begging for admission into the European Economic Community. Greece, Portugal and Spain recently joined the Community and Turkey wishes to do so. Luxembourg is an example of a small country that is still comfortable with the experience of co-existing with larger ones.
It does not automatically follow that the small in any way are jeopardized by a relationship with the large, unless the small countries have no confidence in themselves.
Some of us watched the football games on the weekend. Football teams that were not expected to win did indeed win. If they had gone into the football game with the same sense of insecurity which I hear some Canadians express today, they probably would have been defeated before the game began.
The point is that the essence of the agreement is that we must believe in ourselves. In a perfect world, I would certainly prefer that we had less trade with the United States. While I am uncomfortable with the fact that 77 per cent of our trade is with the United States, I do know that many attempts in the past to redress that have been unsuccessful, despite the intervention of Government in many cases, because it has, quite frankly, been to the economic advantage of producers and consumers in Canada to maintain that trading relationship.
I do not believe we have put all our eggs in one basket. This Government is very much committed to developing trade with the Pacific Rim, as is Canadian industry. For example, when I advised the President of the Canadian Pork Council of my inability to reach him, he told me that he was going to Tokyo to develop markets there for Canadian fresh pork.
We should also stress that the free trade agreement is built within the comprehensive framework of the GATT. The agreement is part of the whole and not meant to stand alone. By working toward both a freer trade agreement with the United States and an improved GATT agreement, the interests of Canadian consumers and producers will be very definitely protected.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Clark) on the excellent presentation he made this afternoon. Since the free trade debate began, we have seen the sides clearly drawn, mainly on political philosophies. This has been evident in the daily newspapers in western Canada, eastern Canada, in the farm papers and in the positions put forward by the spokespersons on free trade.
The political debate that is ranging in Canada over this issue should be more confined to this Chamber and possibly to provincial legislatures throughout Canada, rather than to the degree to which it is engaged in by some of the participants.
There is no doubt that the issue of free trade is a very complex one. However, I think it deserves to be studied carefully by examining the real issues and not participating

November 24, 1987
Adjournment Debate
only in rhetoric, particularly when it is purely political in nature.
The Member did an excellent job of putting forward the position the Government has taken since this debate began.
Of the two or three key issues that I hear raised in discussions about free trade, one is the fact that people do not seem to be totally convinced that we have provided protection, particularly for the supply managed commodities. Perhaps the Hon. Member could comment on the protection that has been put in place for the feather industries and the dairy industries. Perhaps he could also comment on the two-price wheat system that is certainly questioned in western Canada by growers to whom I speak, who want to know the Government's intention with respect to the removal of two-priced wheat.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member has raised a number of important questions. I will try to address them as briefly as possible.
First, 1 believe most Members in the House are aware that the supply management programs remain intact. Furthermore, we have a continuing right to establish new supply management programs in the future. It is important to stress that fact because there are many who feared that they would be destroyed by the agreement. That is not the case.
Second, the quota system for imports in all those supply managed programs remains intact. The Hon. Member referred to the feather industry. In some cases there is an increase in quota, with a maximum of 1.5 per cent which is permitted under the freer trade agreement. 1 believe that is an increase with which most of the industry is comfortable.
The Hon. Member asked me to comment on two-priced wheat. I think the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) and others have made it very clear that whenever that program should be phased out in the future, adequate compensation would be provided to producers, if necessary. However, we believe that it is quite possible that by the time this happens the price will be rising and hopefully the export price will be closer to the domestic price.
Most of the western grain farm community, at least, has responded fairly well to this because domestic wheat constitutes about 8 per cent of our market, and it is the 80 per cent of our wheat which we sell in the world community that is very important to us. That is where we must concentrate our efforts.

speechtext: It being six o'clock, it is my duty to inform the House that, pursuant to Standing Order 82(12), proceedings on the motion have expired.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in the adjournment debate this evening on a matter that is indeed very cherished in the part of the world 1 come from, primarily the constituencies of Saint John and Fundy-Royal. I am delighted that we have such an eminent Parliamentary Secretary with us tonight. I understand he is going to answer on behalf of the Government. I hold him in great esteem. 1 consider him to be one of the most respected, if not the most respected, Parliamentary Secretaries. 1 know he will be fair. 1 know he will be charitable, and I do not say that just because he happens to pay half the rent.
I raised my question regarding the awarding of the next six frigates because of the apparent struggle between Quebec and New Brunswick which 1 consider to be not only degrading but somewhat unpleasant. I fear, as do many New Brunswickers, that an opportunity to build the frigates in a yard that has the expertise and the best offer will be lost as Cabinet participates in a regional struggle which, as most people are aware, has delayed the awarding of the contract.
The case supporting the awarding of the frigate contract to the Saint John shipyard is indeed very strong. The company wants to build all six ships in its yard. It feels it can do so for a package of $1,976 billion, which is a considerable saving of $80 million per ship. I want to point out to you, Madam Speaker, and to all Canadians that this is about $700 million less than the original estimates for this package.
The Saint John yard is the prime contractor of the first batch of frigates. It has developed the technology and has assembled the personnel necessary to construct this class of frigate. In place today is a world class, top notch complement of designers, engineers, program managers and construction workers, all ready and willing to undertake the challenge of constructing the next six frigates. The record of the Saint John yard is excellent. The frigate program now under way is commendable. It is on schedule and within budget. The lead ship should be delivered by October 1989. In an era where we should have no waste contributing to the spiralling deficit we were exposed to because of the previous administration, this is a refreshing revelation.
I want to say that the first phase of the frigate program has been successful in creating jobs in southern New Brunswick and in Saint John. It has injected millions of dollars into the local economy of Atlantic Canada and has stimulated industry and job creation. You may be aware, Madam Speaker, that
November 24, 1987

the shipbuilding industry in southern New Brunswick is critical to the employment and economic expansion of our region. A decline in the shipbuilding industry always hits the local and regional economies very hard and has repercussions throughout every sector.
Defence procurement programs appear to be distributed fairly across Canada. British Columbia is a leading bidder for the half billion dollar ice-breaker contract. The West won the contract to improve the CF-5 fighter jet. Quebec received the CF-18 contract. I am seriously concerned by reports about the confusion surrounding the awarding of the contract. Ministers are reported to be making statements and then retracting them. 1 am concerned about the delay and the apparent regional confrontation within Cabinet. Almost every media account of this issue draws parallels between the awarding of this contract and the awarding of the CF-18 contract. I know Members of Parliament from Quebec are concerned about unemployed shipbuilders and economic opportunities, job creation and high-tech development.
However, a great deal has already been done by the Government to stimulate economic growth in Quebec. I think that we should square up to that fact. For instance, a $55 million grant was provided to improve petrochemical facilities. Under a $100 million federal-provincial agreement Quebec will receive more than 40 per cent of Canada's tourism development budget. A $100 million interest free loan was made available to General Motors. A three-year agreement generating $278 million in federal funds will be used for the purchase of training courses. Close to 3,000 jobs have been created in the aerospace sector which has received almost $200 million in federal contributions.
It may not be well recognized by the majority of Canadians, but Quebec has already handsomely benefited by the lion's share of the 1983 frigate contract. Although Saint John was a prime contractor, some $972 million will be spent in Quebec providing 12,180 man-years of work compared to $650 million to be spent in the Atlantic region providing 8,100 man-years of work.
The Saint John yard has calculated that splitting the work between Saint John and Quebec will cost an extra $480 million. As Canadians, this is something that we do not look forward to. We could almost purchase another frigate with the money that would be saved.
The Saint John yard has established itself as Canada's centre for the design and construction of navy vessels. It has created a centre of excellence. I strongly urge the Government to make a decision as soon as possible and award a six frigate contract to the yard that offers both the expertise and the best deal, the Saint John Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Company. Canadians do not want to see Cabinet bend to political pressures and replay the CF-18 scenario.
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Stewart (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to respond not only to my colleague, but one of my dearest friends, someone who represents so ably the constituents of Fundy-Royal. I might point out that the Hon. Member is equally at home on the range, and always shares in pulling his weight in all endeavours, whether they be for frigates, or for his constituents in any way, shape, or form.
I understand the concerns of the Hon. Member, and I do not think there is anyone who could have put the problem more loquaciously. I will attempt to sum up the current situation relative to the awarding of the contract for construction of the second batch of patrol frigates.
As mentioned previously in the House by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Cote), I will repeat again for those still unaware that the decision has not yet been taken by the Government.
I would like to clarify for the House the importance of this contract. As has been pointed out, we are talking about billions of dollars. It is a total expenditure of $3.5 billion. I think that the Government has every reason to insist on carefully weighing all aspects of a defence expenditure of this magnitude. I can assure my hon. colleague that such an important decision will not be made in haste. When it is made, it will be a decision that will prove beneficial for all Canadians.
As in all decisions on the awarding of contracts, Phase II of the Canadian Patrol Frigate Program will be based on clear criteria: the responsiveness of defence requirements, the expertise and technical capacity of the contractor, and the costs and regional and economic benefits associated with the project.
As the Minister of Supply and Services and others have stated in the House, and as a means of calming the anxieties of my colleague from Fundy-Royal, I repeat that the contract for the second phase of frigates will be made according to operational requirements, the best value against the cost, the efficiency of the contractor, the time frame proposed, and the industrial spin-offs.
Of all people, I can well appreciate the strong belief of the Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal that the contract should be awarded to Saint John Shipbuilding. Even though my fellow Member represents the interests of Atlantic Canada, he must also realize that the role of the Government is to respond in the best interests of the country as a whole, and to determine the best way to ensure regional development.
