Madam Speaker, I wish to follow up on the question that yesterday I directed to the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Vezina). She was asked questions not only by me, but by my colleague, the Hon.

November 24, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud). The Hon. Minister has been unable to answer any of the four specific questions that have been put forward by either my colleague from Westmorland-Kent, or myself.
These questions concerned the transport industry in relation to the free trade agreement which Canada will sign and enter into with the Americans. I sympathize with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on his bad luck in selecting a competent Minister of State for Transport. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) is a great joker, but he has failed to come to grips with the complex issue of transportation. The terrible thing about it is that we have had a succession of Ministers of State for Transport, one after another, who have shown irresponsibility or incompetence. That is the situation exactly, when we look at the answers given by the Minister of State for Transport yesterday.
The only bright spot in the Department is the Parliamentary Secretary who has shown some understanding of the problems and a willingness to listen to representations in all meetings of the Standing Committee on Transport and in answering questions in the House yesterday and today.
In reality, the deal with the Americans will be terrible for the trucking industry. While the Government tried to make people believe that it was a marvellous deal, the reality is that it will be a terrible one for the trucking industry.
Raymond Cope, President of the Ontario Trucking Association says that 100,000 jobs in the province's trucking industry are at stake. He went on to say: "We see the potential to devastate the Ontario trucking industry". Mr. Ron Downey, President of the Manitoba Trucking Association says that the Canadian and U.S. trucking industries are not playing on a level playing field. He went on to say:
Certain tax and immigration changes should have been put in place before
the trade accord.
Mr. Don Norquay, Chairman of the Manitoba Motor Transport Board, said the following:
The draft agreement would not allow Canada to take any action to prevent
complete domination of our highway transport industry by Americans.
These people represent the industry and they are absolutely furious at the lack of appropriate responsibility and initiative on the part of the Minister of Transport.

Yesterday, I asked the Minister of State (Transport) (Mrs. Vezina) to tell us whether the Canadian provinces will be able to refuse license applications made by United States truckers based in states that do not give Canadian truckers a fair deal. This was a very simple question calling for a yes or no. The Minister was not even able to tell me whether such would be the case. This matter is very important for the workers in the Canadian trucking industry, for 43 American states continue to regulate the trucking industry within their own respective
jurisdictions. Under their regulations, Canadian trucking firms cannot transport merchandise or goods from one point to another within the same state: Michigan, New York and Pennsylvania, three major border states, are part of this group. Because of these regulations, for instance, in the State of New York, a Canadian firm cannot transport goods from New York City to Rochester. On the other hand, a firm based in the United States will be able to transport goods, say, from Toronto to Windsor because of the deregulation of the trucking transport industry which the Conservative government will impose on Ontario and the other Canadian provinces through Bill C-19. This right provides access to extremely profitable trucking services and will mean enormous profits for the American companies which take over contracts from the Canadian trucking industry. This is a far cry from fair competition, one of the basic principles and objectives of the so-called Free Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States.
The truckers would like the provincial transport commissions to keep their other regulatory powers, as this would give them some reciprocity as far as regulations are concerned when the American truckers ask for authorization to move goods from one province to another. The commission would be able to verify whether Canadian carriers have been refused a similar operating permit in the state or region of origin of the American trucker submitting an application to transport goods in Canada.
This is what I asked the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Vezina) yesterday, and she was unable to give me an answer. I trust that the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to clarify the situation this evening because, and I shall close with this, the Canadian Trucking Association has suggested, to correct this situation which could be extremely unfair to the Canadian trucking industry, that the final text of the schedule on transport in this agreement between Canada and the United States give at the very least the same status to the reciprocity provisions as to the principle of national treatment. This is the minimum required, and I trust that the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to give us an affirmative answer.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in spite of the nice words from the Member opposite I must challenge his allegations against the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie). As my friend opposite knows, Ministers are worked to death in this country and the Minister of Transport has handled his portfolio with great aplomb and also with enormous hard work and dedication. Absolute major Bills, Bill C-18, C-19 and C-21 changing the public policy of this nation were rammed through this House under the tutelage of the present Minister of Transport.

By the Parliamentary Secretary.
November 24, 1987

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
With respect to Ontario trucking, there is no doubt some Ontario truckers are worried about the free trade agreement but not all Ontario truckers are. As well, let me say to my hon. friend that in Alberta that industry has been deregulated and subject to the market-place for many years and has thrived. There is no reason at all why Ontario truckers with their entrepreneurship and ingenuity cannot go into the United States and compete, and compete with anyone in the world.
My friend has pointed out that some 43 states in the U.S.A. have refused licences to subsidiaries of Canadian trucking firms which want to carry freight only within those specific states. He also points out that some of our provinces as a result of Bill C-19 will for at least five years come under the reverse onus clause, and after that it will be a fit, willing and able test which anyone can meet. Even at that time, U.S. truckers will not be able to operate here interprovincially at will. They would, as now, have to establish themselves as Canadian companies, engage Canadian citizens, have a subsidiary corporation or at least a Canadian corporation, pay income tax here and compete within the competition milieu of Canada. I think we can whip them as Alberta truckers have in the U.S. They have done well so I am not quite as worried as my friend opposite, although he raises the point very well.
If discrimination of restrictive practices by states against Canadian carriers can be proven, the Government could invoke that clause in Bill C-19, which my friend talked about eloquently when the Bill was going through, the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, which permits retaliation if remedial action is not taken through consultation. I can assure the Hon. Member that the Government under the Minister of Transport or, indeed, any Government will retaliate if the Americans do not treat our truckers fairly.
FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS-PRINCIPAL SAVINGS AND TRUST BANKRUPTCY/REPORTED TRANSFER OF FUNDS

Madam Speaker, on August 12, I put a question to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) concerning the Principal Savings and Trust Company. At that time, two corporations in the Province of Alberta had claimed bankruptcy; namely, First Investors and Associated Investors. It should be stated clearly that those companies fell under the jurisdiction of provincial regulation and not federal regulation. However, they were part and parcel of a corporate network or web of companies operating that type of business.
In fact, the Principal Savings and Trust Company, which is interlinked with those two provincially-regulated companies, is regulated federally under the auspices of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. At that time, I was hoping that the Minister could provide to Members of the House information which would shed light on some of the obvious questions that had been put and are still wanting for answers.
Adjournment Debate
We have learned in recent weeks and indeed in recent months of investigations that have been launched by provincial administrations. We have also learned to our dismay that a great number of Canadians from across Canada have been affected negatively by the operations of Principal Savings and Trust and the other companies to which it was linked. In fact, 50,000 to 60,000 of those Canadians have lost many personal investments.
The point here is that Canadians in my own Province of Nova Scotia and indeed my own constituency as well as people from Alberta, parts of British Columbia and all across Canada have lost a great deal of money. The Government's claim is that this falls under the jurisdiction of the provincial Government and not the federal Government, therefore its responsibility has been met. However, the Parliamentary Secretary is aware that audits were done by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation of Principal Savings and Trust. The Minister, under the guise of confidentiality, has refused to table those audits.
I realize the importance of confidentiality within the business sector, but what ought to be of paramount importance, not only to the Government but indeed to the managers and business leaders in that sector of the economy is that we must know and know clearly all the facts and all the details surrounding the collapse of Principal Savings and Trust and the associated companies. It is only through that knowledge that Canadians as well as business people involved in that business can have confidence that the system we have in place is in fact serving and meeting the needs and objectives about which Canadians feel very strongly. The Government has persistently and consistently said no to making that information available.
Government Members are also aware that some very misleading practices have taken place. We would like to know what the Government has communicated to the Province of Alberta with regard to those practices. Has it given the file to the Minister responsible in the Province of Alberta? Has it given the file to the commercial fraud section of the RCMP? Has it done an investigation under Consumer and Corporate Affairs?
I think that Canadians are losing thousands upon thousands of dollars because of mismanagement and that the Government is attempting to protect, under the guise of confidentiality, what took place weeks, months and maybe even years ago in those companies.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary is able to inform not only Canadians in general but those 60,000 Canadians who have lost money in Principal Savings and Trust about whether or not it is prepared to co-operate with provincial Governments in fully reimbursing those people. I hope he is able to tell us that the Government will provide all of the details and remove

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to respond to the Hon. Member on behalf of the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin). As the Hon. Member and all other Hon. Members know, these have been very difficult times for the financial industry in general. We have all been saddened to see the failure of several banks and trust companies. Those failures have naturally raised questions as to the adequacy of the regulatory framework. I very much appreciate the concerns of the Hon. Member which he has raised before in this House as well as tonight.
From his remarks the Hon. Member recognizes that the Principal Group and its affiliated companies, except for an inactive federally-incorporated insurance company, were under the supervision of the Alberta Government. The federal Government's only involvement was through the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation insuring Principal Savings and Trust Company. As a result of that role, depositors in that trust company will be completely protected up to the insurance ceiling of $60,000.
As Hon. Members are all too painfully aware, many investment contract holders claim misrepresentations were made to them by representatives of First Investors Corporation and Associated Investors Corporation in the sale of investment contract certificates. I note, as the Hon. Member did, that the Province of Alberta announced certain measures to bring the affairs of the two investment companies under the control and scrutiny of the courts and the two companies' creditors. It is my understanding that Government has since expanded its inquiry to include a complete review of all inter-company transactions among the Principal Group of companies.
As Hon. Members know, the federal Government has placed a very high priority on addressing the problems of federally-regulated financial institutions. The Hon. Minister of State for Finance, on December 18, 1986, released a policy paper entitled "New Directions for the Financial Sector". The Government has already completed the first two stages of the process with the recent passage of Bill C-42 and Bill C-56.
The third stage of the reform package will introduce legislative amendments which should help prevent circumstances of the type currently causing investment contract holders in the uninsured affiliates of the Principal Group so much concerned. In this regard, federally-regulated institutions will, with limited exceptions, be prohibited from engaging in transactions with their affiliated companies. In addition, the actions of corporate officers and directors will be subject to stringent performance requirements to control conflict of interest and other insider activity. I would also note that the federal proposals contain a directors' policy which will ensure that one-third of the directors are unaffiliated and no more than 15 per cent of the directors on the boards of federally-regulated financial institutions are insiders.
I believe we have made considerable progress with Bill C-42 and Bill C-56 and that the third phase of this program will address the majority of concerns presented this evening by the Hon. Member.
